title: Basic mobile coverage is now law, but only Starlink can offer it
text:
Amid a busy sitting week in Canberra last week, you would be forgiven for missing a new law that could affect the lives of millions of Australians.

For the first time telecommunications companies will be required to provide a baseline level of mobile coverage across the country.

But a lot of the details are yet to be worked out and the timeframes yet to be settled.

What's new?

While 98 per cent of Australians use their mobiles to make calls, coverage is only available across less than a third of country's landmass, and sometimes only through one provider.

Communications Minister Anika Wells said the new Universal Outdoor Mobile Obligation (UOMO) bill would ensure Australians were covered "nearly anywhere" outdoors.

As federal communications minister, Anika Wells has a lot of discretion about how the new laws will work. (ABC News: Joel Wilson)

"It requires mobile network operators, who are Telstra, Optus and TPG, to provide baseline outdoor voice and text coverage throughout Australia," she said.

"Secondly, it gives me as minister the ability to set standards regarding mobile services, so things like reliability or fault rectification."

The bill updates the existing Universal Service Obligation, which only mandates access to fixed lines and payphones.

Telcos could meet their obligation using land-based infrastructure, such as mobile towers, but it is expected vast areas will be covered by Low Earth Orbit satellites, known as LEO Sats.

How does it work?

The direct-to-device or direct-to-mobile technology is different to how many Australians might already use satellite to access internet through NBN's Sky Muster or Elon Musk's Starlink, which requires a receiver.

To get reception direct to a mobile it needs to be able to connect directly to satellite, which means you need to be outside.

SpaceX courts Australian investors Australian government officials are privately flagging the risks posed by the country's growing reliance on Starlink.

It is technology that only Starlink can currently provide, but Ms Wells said the new law was about "getting ahead of the game".

"We're hoping to put in place the conditions through these laws that allow Australian entrepreneurship to create, innovate and come up with technology that we can select over things like Starlink," she said.

" But at the moment, regional Australians need connectivity … so we need to get them a better service, we need to ensure that telcos lift their game. "

Telstra already provides a direct-to-device satellite text messaging service through Starlink.

But it uses existing spectrum and is available to certain customers on certain phones and cannot be used to contact Triple Zero (000).

Industry and consumer advocates have broadly welcomed the bill, but there are also parts they take issue with, for very different reasons.

Luke Coleman says the technology needed to meet the expectations of the bill is still in its infancy. (ABC News)

"Direct-to-device technology is a very new technology, it has not been widely tested or commercialised," Australian Telecommunications Alliance chief executive Luke Coleman said.

Mr Coleman said the "special spectrum required for satellite services" was yet to be allocated and the technology still needed to be integrated into networks.

"There's still a few things that the industry needs to get through before this becomes a normal operational commercial service," he said.

He said with no plans for Australia to launch its own sovereign LEO Sat capability, telcos would be left to come up with commercial agreements.

"We are talking about services in areas that are by definition not commercially viable," he said.

"So, a real part of the challenge is how these can be sustainably funded."

The Australian Communications Consumer Advocacy Network (ACCAN) took a very different view.

Carol Bennett argues the technology to meet basic mobile access already exists, but is worried about the cost for consumers. (ABC News: John Gunn)

"[The satellite technology] is already being used around the world," the network's chief executive Carol Bennett said.

"We don't want it to become situation where only those who can afford to access this get access because … it'll lock them out of being able to participate fully in the economy if they can't achieve access to this technology."

What's still to be worked out?

There is a lot of ministerial discretion in this bill.

The minister for communications will have the power to determine what the baseline will be in terms of quality of calls and texts, where it will reach, what it will cost, how it is funded, if it will include Triple Zero capabilities, when it will be delivered and fault rectification measures.

Ms Bennett said while ACCAN supported the bill, there were "missed opportunities" by not supporting amendments proposed by the Greens and independent senator Jacqui Lambie.

"Those amendments that ensure that reliability and performance standards and domestic mobile roaming can happen now," she said.

"Both measures would make a huge difference to the uplift in the reliability of telecommunication services, particularly in the regions, and to the safety net that's available to consumers when they don't have a provider that delivers them connectivity and they can roam onto another network."

Domestic roaming to be key focus of fresh ACCC inquiry Consumer advocates are disappointed that the ACCC will take 12 months to investigate domestic roaming.

Ms Wells said she wanted to consult industry and stakeholders before setting those standards, but pointed to a separate bill passed last week that increased penalties for telco breaches by 40 times to more than $10 million.

"I don't want to promise things we can't deliver," she said.

"We need to strike a balance between improving mobile services whilst acknowledging that these networks can be complex, can be expensive to maintain."

As for how Triple Zero obligations would interact with the new mobile standards, that is still to be worked out too with a broader review of the Triple Zero Custodian currently underway.

When will it start?

The default start date in the bill is December 31, 2027, but there is discretion for the minister to delay that until the end of 2030.

Ms Wells said she was "ambitious" and wanted it in place by December 1 next year.

The Australian Telecommunications Alliance indicated that was unlikely.

"On the current trajectory, we still need the spectrum to be allocated for this service to become operational," Mr Coleman said.

"Things would weigh in favour of delaying the start date until the market has developed a bit more."

title: Outstations and town camps struggle with damage from 'scary' storm
text:
Central Australian residents say the poor quality of many homes in remote outstations and town camps has amplified damage after a storm whipped through southern parts of the Northern Territory last Monday.

Trees were uprooted, there were widespread power outages and roofs were ripped from homes as winds of up to 96 kilometres an hour, a two minute drive from the remote community of Hermannsburg, was significantly damaged during the storm.

The Western Arrarnta woman was in Canberra during the severe weather event, but said her children phoned her to tell her of the damage.

"They said it was a mini cyclone or hurricane … and it was a bit scary," she said.

"Trees were pulled out from the ground, rain just falling over the houses."

Ms Malbunka said the power went out in most outstations around the region and families were struggling to feed themselves, but electricity was restored in about two days.

Strong winds and rain destroyed Maryanne Malbunka's homeland property near Hermannsburg. (Supplied: Maryanne Malbunka)

The health worker said existing challenges with housing in many remote outstations made the homes more vulnerable to storm and many residents in the region were "struggling".

"Maybe when we get more rain or more storms like that our houses will be flown out, because we're only living in a tin shed, and some of those brick houses aren't being renovated or looked at properly," she said.

The remote location means storm clean-up will be difficult. (Supplied: Maryanne Malbunka)

Ms Malbunka said outstation residents would need to make many trips to the tip to clean up their properties, which would be costly due to the high price of fuel.

Town camps also damaged

A Northern Territory government spokesperson said four public housing properties were uninhabitable due to damage and there were 59 storm-related repair jobs across public housing in town, including five town camps.

The spokesperson said the government was "prioritising relocating" families in affected homes to alternative public housing while the houses were repaired.

Caleb Doolan says he had to throw out food after his power went out in the storm. (ABC Alice Springs: Xavier Martin)

Mpwetyerre/Abbott's Town Camp resident Caleb Doolan said his home lost power and children in the town camp were scared.

"We had to chuck everything out from the fridge," he said.

"It was hard for us."

Mr Doolan said the storm was another blow to the town camp, which was still recovering from floods earlier in the year.

title: RLWC quick hits: Ponga's power, Tonga's triumph and Fiji's sunny day
text:
The first week of the Rugby League World Cup is in the books with stars new and old making statements across the tournament.

From the classic opener between Australia and New Zealand to Tonga's statement win over England and Papua New Guinea's handy victory over Lebanon there's plenty for the international football fan to sink their teeth into.

Here are the quick hits from the opening round.

1. Kalyn Ponga holds New Zealand's hopes in his hands

Ponga scored a double for New Zealand before departing late with a broken arm. (Getty Images: Matt King)

Over the past few months Kalyn Ponga has made a transformation from someone who can play great into a great player and if his World Cup is over due to a broken arm not only will the tournament be far poorer without him he might take New Zealand's title hopes home with him.

Ponga was magnificent in his Kiwi debut on Friday night, scoring two tries and running for 254 metres as he continued the form that helped drive Newcastle to the grand final earlier this month.

World Cup opener a reminder of Australia's glory days There was a time when Test matches were rugby league's biggest, best and bloodiest spectacles, and last night's World Cup opener between Australia and New Zealand was a reminder of those days.

His battles with Australia's Reece Walsh will take some beating as the defining memory from the entire World Cup even as New Zealand fell to a frustrating defeat where they dominated every major stat but the scoreboard.

Ponga has undergone surgery and will remain in camp but if his transcendent year is over, things might have peaked early for the Kiwis.

Keano Kini, a fine fullback in his own right, was terrific in New Zealand's Pacific Championship win last year and has the work rate and running game to break any match open.

But he is not Kalyn Ponga, who is not rare but unique. That means there's nobody else like him.

2. Speed can kill for lightning Samoan backline

Fa'alogo scored four tries off the bench for Samoa in their big win over France. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

It's a measure of the depth Samoa enjoy that Su'a Fa'alogo, Melbourne's player of the year and one of the most dynamic attacking weapons in the sport, could only crack a bench spot for their first match.

Even so, Samoa proved they could strike from anywhere at any time and through almost any player — Jermaine McEwan's 50 metre solo effort will be one of the best efforts of the entire World Cup.

But after Fa'alogo was pitched into the action early following an injury to Deine Mariner and finished with four tries, three try assists and seven linebreaks in this thumping victory it's clear he can act as the Toa's wildcard as they look to emulate 2022's brilliant run to the final.

Just where the Storm fullback fits into the side remains to be seen — Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow is a brilliant fullback in his own right and Fa'alogo's unfamiliarity with playing wing could be targeted by more dangerous opposition.

But speed can kill and when Fa'alogo is out there Samoa have enough to run and gun with anybody.

3. Future is now for Papua New Guinea

The looming presence of the PNG Chiefs is the subtext beneath every Papua New Guinea game in this World Cup and after this impressive win it seems they've landed a good one in Gairo Voro.

The 23-year old five-eighth is coming off a monster season with London Broncos in the English second division, where he scored 39 tries in 31 games to claim the competition's player of the year award.

He took that good form into this victory, scoring a long range try and creating another with his speed and footwork standing out against a Cedars side with plenty of NRL experience.

Tapping into as much local talent as possible will be crucial and if Voro's improvement continues very well could be one of their early success stories.

4. Powerful Tongan statement a long time coming

Tonga ran roughshod over a disappointing England side. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

Tonga's fourth win over a Tier 1 nation is by far their most dominant — the margin of victory is just one point more than the combined margin of all three previous wins.

Even though they've won just one of their past nine matches, have been building to a dominant performance like this for some time.

All nine of those games were against Australia, England, New Zealand or Samoa, and Tonga are now experience the gain from the pain of those defeats.

Tonga now have one foot in the semi-finals. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

The attacking cohesion between regulars like Isaiya Katoa, Haumole Olakau'atu and veteran Tui Lolohea was plain to see, as was the defensive combinations that held England to just two tries despite enjoying far better of the field position, and shows that the benefits of regular matches extends beyond than simply winning and losing.

Tonga have hit the ground running but will still have improvement in them. With a semi-final spot essentially at their mercy after this win, it's a good spot to be in.

England, by contrast, have paid the price for the same flaw that cost them in last year's Ashes series — a lack of spark inside the attacking 20. They've scored just 30 points across their past four matches and their inability to strike has them on the verge of their earliest ever World Cup exit.

5. Fiji makes hay while the sun shines

Solomone Saukuru of Fiji scores a try during the 2026 Men's Rugby League World Cup. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner )

With matches against Australia and New Zealand to come this might be as good as it gets for Fiji in this World Cup but you'd be hard-pressed to find a better day in the sun for the Bati than their opener against the Cook Islands.

After their women's side, the Bulikula, came within a whisker of pulling off a remarkable upset against New Zealand in just their ninth match ever they lined the tunnel to sing the men's team onto the field as they were led out by Fiji legend Akuila Uate carrying the national flag.

It was a potent mix of past and future combining in the present and didn't just Fiji duly responded, they looked good doing it.

Halves Kurt Donogohoe and Brandon Wakeham, who both played in last year's Pacific Bowl tournament together, showed the benefits of their combination with five try assists between them and Manly lock Caleb Navale was excellent in the middle of the field.

There will be harder matches to come but expect Fiji to hold the gloves up.

They haven't played a Tier 1 nation since the last World Cup but they have the talent, experience and cohesion to make Australia sweat for at least a little while.

title: Small-scale florists hope to fill gap for romantics in Kununurra
text:
There is perhaps no easier, more sure-fire way to brighten a loved one's day than to send a fresh bunch of flowers. That is of course, if they live in a city.

It is a different story for those living in remote towns and communities.

Perth resident Gerald Contreras is acutely aware of this challenge as he now struggles to surprise his partner who lives 3,000 kilometres north of him in Kununurra.

Until recently, one major supplier of flowers serviced the town's permanent population of about 5,500 people.

Gerald Contreras and his partner Cesarina Fitzgerald live 3,000 kilometres apart. (Supplied: Gerald Contreras)

Mr Contreras said he sent his partner flowers at least once every two months, but that ended when the florist business closed.

"Being Kununurra, a very small town, there's not many options to surprise my partner with love gestures," he said.

"Not even anything like ordering a simple meal; so, flowers was one of the very few ways I could show affection, love, and surprise my partner."

End of an era

For three decades Diane and Chris Robinson were the main players in Kununurra when it came to flowers.

They would grow their own blooms when the weather permitted and trucked up flowers from Perth.

"During the wet season, when we can only grow tropical flowers. We did bring flowers from down south and gradually it just turned into all year," Ms Robinson said.

"We can't grow roses … and also the Australian native flowers are not very good here."

While demand was consistent, the pair struggled to find a long-term shop assistant to sell their flowers.

Diane Robinson sold flowers in Kununurra for more than 30 years. (ABC Kimberley: Jess Baker)

With the Robinsons are looking to retire, a decision needed to be made.

"We're going down that retirement path, so they [the flowers] were pretty easy to [let go of] because we couldn't get a florist," Ms Robinson said.

"If we perhaps had somebody that was staying, we wouldn't have shut the shop quite so quickly."

Diane Robinson says growing flowers in Kununurra is interesting, with only tropical flowers able to be grown in the wet season. (ABC Kimberley: Jess Baker)

Selling flowers on smaller scale

Meanwhile, Bianca Brown has begun assembling and supplying flower bouquets while also running an agricultural transport business.

Ms Brown said she wanted to fill a gap in the market.

"Already I'm at the point where I probably could put somebody else on and I'll probably look at scaling up next year and seeing where it goes," she said.

Ms Brown was sourcing flowers locally and from Perth, and was looking forward to seeing what types of flowers she could grow herself.

Bianca Brown recently started selling floral arrangements in Kununurra. (Supplied: Bianca Brown)

Mr Contreras said he was eager to use Ms Brown's flower delivery service.

"Beyond text messages and calls and video dates, I'm keen to try the new florist who is in a much smaller capacity," he said.

"When I did surprise my partner by flying up I was looking all over town for flowers, and couldn't find any, even in person.

"But the florist did restock the next day with a small amount of flowers. I think I bought almost half the stock."

Sophie Cooke's outback flower patch is open to the public on Saturday dry season mornings. (ABC Kimberley: Jess Baker)

There is one other option to buy blooms in the remote town, but only in the dry season and on Saturdays.

Sophie Cooke lets people visit her family farm and pick flowers themselves to buy.

Ms Cooke said her customers mostly bought flowers for their homes, but also visited the patch for special occasions.

She said a number of residents had started arranging flowers to meet the town's needs, but there was scope to grow more flowers and the industry.

title: Cindy Crawford 'beyond heartbroken' to lose son Presley Gerber
text:
American supermodel Cindy Crawford has posted a tribute on social media to her son Presley Gerber, who recently died aged 27.

"We are beyond heartbroken to lose our beloved son and brother," Crawford's Instagram post said.

"We feel so blessed to have had Presley in our lives for 27 years. He is a sweet, beautiful soul who loved and is loved, now and forever."

Loading Instagram content

The 27-year-old was Crawford's only son with her businessman husband, Rande Gerber, and the older brother of model-actor Kaia.

Gerber died in September at a rehab facility, according to the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner.

Crawford thanked fans for their support, saying: "We are grateful for the outpouring of love and support from so many who know and love our family and even strangers who feel our pain."

Sister, Kaia Gerber, also posted a tribute to "Prez" shortly afterwards.

"You know how much I loved being your sister. It has always been, and will forever be, my favourite thing about myself," she said.

" You believed people were inherently good because, Presley, you are inherently good. "

Presley Gerber worked on campaigns and did runway shows for brands such as Calvin Klein and Dolce & Gabbana.

In 2018, he appeared alongside his mother in Pepsi's Super Bowl LII commercial.

Kaia Gerber posted on Instagram about her brother. (Supplied: Kaia Gerber)

He had previously opened up about his struggles with mental health.

In an Instagram post in November, he said he started a series called Mental Health Mondays, saying: "The goal was to spark real conversations about the stuff most people hide."

In August, Kaia Gerber spoke about her brother's struggles in an interview with Vogue magazine.

When something like that happens in a family, it "kind of levels everyone", she said.

ABC/Reuters

title: Inside the 'ghost city' designed to become Indonesia's new capital
text:
Loading...

Carved into the rainforests of Borneo, a brand-new city is taking shape.

It features a presidential palace, modern offices, residential towers and wide, open roads.

Loading...

This is Nusantara, the futuristic city designed to become Indonesia's new capital.

But there is one big problem.

Loading...

The city is quiet. Almost too quiet.

It was designed to hold 1.2 million people by 2029. So far, only about 10,000 have moved in.

Indonesia has spent billions on building a new capital. But there are fears the world's fourth-largest country's bet may not pay off.

Read the story in Bahasa Indonesia

Nusantara stands in stark contrast to Indonesia's current capital, Jakarta.

The heaving metropolis, home to almost 42 million people, was last year declared the world's most populous city, overtaking Tokyo to secure the title.

Jakarta's issues are well documented. It is notorious for its poor air quality and its heavily congested traffic, which is among the worst in the world.

There are also concerns about overcrowding: Greater Jakarta has 1.5 times as many people as Australia, living in a space about 1,200 times smaller than Australia's landmass.

But the city's biggest problem is that it is sinking.

Loading...

In 2025, Jakarta overtook Tokyo to become the world's most populous city, with 42 million residents, according to UN estimates. ( )

Jakarta is infamous for its bumper-to-bumper traffic and hours-long traffic jams. ( )

Behind the towering office and residential complexes, many of Jakarta's inhabitants eke out a living in makeshift communities like this. ( )

About 40 per cent of Jakarta sits below sea level, with a sea wall in the city's north serving as a line of defence against tidal floods.

But parts of the north still regularly flood in the rainy season.

There have been many proposals over the decades to move Indonesia's capital, stretching as far back as the 1950s.

But in 2019, former president Joko Widodo, known commonly as Jokowi, made the ambitious call to build a glittering new capital city deep in the jungle of Borneo.

Utopia in the jungle

Much of the thick jungle that covered the Nusantara site was cleared to make way for the new city. ( )

The city of IKN, or Nusantara, is more than 1,200 kilometres from Jakarta, in the province of East Kalimantan.

Nusantara is seen as somewhat of a legacy project for Jokowi, who was highly popular during his time as president.

It was pitched as the true centre of Indonesia's thousands of islands and an engine for future economic growth.

It was also expected to wrest control from the Java-centric decision-makers of Jakarta.

Construction began on the forest city in 2022, with the aim of it becoming a hub for 1.9 million people by Indonesia's 100th anniversary in 2045.

It was expected to cost about $45 billion.

In 2024, Jokowi celebrated Indonesia's Independence Day at the newly constructed palace in Nusantara, after the city had been partially inaugurated and named as the new capital.

But a lot can change in two years.

One man's legacy is another's debt

Former leader Joko Widodo poses for a selfie with President Prabowo Subianto. ( )

Jokowi spent about 43 trillion IDR — roughly $3.5 billion — on Nusantara in 2024.

But after President Prabowo Subianto took office, the annual budget for the city was slashed to 13 trillion IDR in 2025 and again to 6.3 trillion IDR in 2026.

Prabowo had pitched himself as a president who would continue Jokowi's agenda, but analysts have observed a widening rift between the two men.

He has shifted large portions of the budget to his signature policies, including a nationwide school meals program, and has not spoken much about Nusantara's development.

During the 2025 State of the Nation address, Prabowo mentioned it once. This year, he did not speak about it at all.

A report in Agence France-Presse last year quoted an anonymous official involved in the construction of Nusantara, saying "Prabowo feels that this is not his legacy."

President Prabowo Subianto has been pursuing his own signature projects in recent years. ( )

When Prabowo visited Nusantara early this year, he stayed just one night in the city.

He has signed a presidential regulation that aims to make Nusantara the "political capital" by 2028, to coincide with the completion of official buildings.

But Indonesia's Constitutional Court ruled this year that Jakarta would remain the official capital until Prabowo signs an additional presidential decree.

That decision prompted considerable discussion.

Would Nusantara become a definitive new capital for 2 million Indonesians? Would it simply become a hub for different branches of government?

Or might it be abandoned in 2028, in the lead-up to a 2029 election?

Living in a political experiment

Ranty Wiyati is adjusting to her new life in Nusantara but is optimistic about the city's potential. ( )

While the wider Nusantara area, which includes dozens of villages and sub-districts, has a population of 147,000, far fewer live in the inner core of the newly developed city.

The brand-new residential towers dotted around Nusantara are home to about 1,800 public servants and defence and security personnel.

The ABC received permission to visit Nusantara from the Nusantara Capital Authority, or OIKN, which manages the development of the city.

For young OIKN worker Ranty Wiyati, living in Nusantara is a big change of pace from the bustling streets of Jakarta.

"You can't deny that it is [quiet]," she said.

"It might not be as busy as Jakarta, and there aren't as many entertainment options, but that's better for our mental health.

"We get creative with ways to stay off social media … we do things like journalling, chatting, holding book clubs."

OIKN is hiring young workers like Ranty to move to Nusantara, while government departments have been slowly transferring workers to the city.

Traffic lights and new facilities wait for the arrival of hundreds of thousands of new residents to Nusantara. ( )

Relocating young government workers to Nusantara may help others follow. ( )

Civil servants make up the majority of permanent residents in Nusantara. ( )

"I chose Nusantara because I thought it would be a new living laboratory for Indonesia," Ranty said, echoing language used by OIKN's chief Basuki Hadimuljono.

"We're hoping that more public servants can be relocated here soon to make the place a bit livelier."

The ABC met Ranty at one of the handful of coffee shops in Nusantara, before taking an electric bus that runs on a loop through the city, passing several hospitals and two hotels.

Shopping centres are slated to be built in the coming years.

Nusantara has attracted some tourists but few Indonesians have decided to make the new capital home. ( )

At an outlook in the city, tourists were singing the city's praises.

The ambitious project is a source of great national pride for Indonesians like Darmiyah. ( )

"Seeing this makes me feel really proud," Darmiyah, from South Kalimantan, said.

Yuda is among a handful of Indonesian tourists keen to see the splendour of the new capital. ( )

"We took a bus for about 12 hours," Yuda, also from South Kalimantan, said.

"The development is really grand. It makes total sense for this to be the national capital moving forward."

Ranty can drink water straight from the taps in her apartment thanks to the filtration systems installed across the city, something almost impossible to do in Jakarta without risking getting sick.

Nusantara is also aiming to be much greener than Jakarta, thanks to compulsory recycling and monitoring of water and electricity use.

"It's a real shame when people call this a ghost city, or talk like that in the media," Ranty said.

"Nusantara is a great opportunity, especially for the younger generation, to build something more ideal from the ground up.

"While we know there aren't many here right now, once the president moves here, that'll be a major turning point."

But while those inside Nusantara remain optimistic, some in Jakarta wonder whether the project will pay off.

Fears new city could become 'white elephant'

The imposing Garuda Palace is the centrepiece of the new administrative capital. ( )

The $45 billion for Jokowi's vision was expected to be covered by 80 per cent private investment, along with 20 per cent government spending.

CELIOS economist Bhima Yudhistira said investor appetite remained low due to geopolitical conditions, rising interest rates and policy risks.

"Nusantara risks becoming a 'white elephant' — an expensive project with minimal impact," he said.

"[It] could end up as a stranded asset, as the state budget may only suffice for basic building maintenance."

He said Prabowo's lack of commitment and his rift with Jokowi meant the project was now a "political gamble."

Public policy expert Agus Pambagio said funding cuts and the court decision had also slowed progress.

"It's developing, but it's not as fast as before," Agus said.

"These are different political parties, different people under the presidents … the style of leadership is different."

Agus doubts Nusantara will be Indonesia's capital by 2028, but OIKN officials remain confident.

"As the old saying goes, the dogs bark, but the caravan moves on," OIKN deputy Dr Alimuddin said.

"To this day, we have full support from the government.

"Does the government need to say in the media, 'We support this?' That's not necessary."

"What matters most is not talking, but keeping the financial support and construction running smoothly."

The network of wide boulevards that bisects the new city still remain largely devoid of traffic. ( )

Life in Nusantara's new apartment buildings is a far cry from the crowded and chaotic conditions of Jakarta. ( )

OIKN Deputy Dr Alimuddin rejects suggestions that Nusantara won't become the new capital. ( )

OIKN said private investors had so far committed $6 billion to Nusantara, and that another $10 billion had come from public-private partnerships.

A lot of people are eagerly awaiting 2028 to see whether Prabowo will issue that presidential decree making Nusantara the political capital.

As construction continues, an enormous steel sculpture shaped like Indonesia's national symbol, the Garuda, a winged, mythical eagle-like bird, watches over the city.

The next year will be a pivotal one for local and foreign investors.

Will Nusantara live up to the original dream of a thriving, populated forest city — or will the massive Garuda remain a mighty monument to a failed legacy project?

title: Bullara Station finds 'silver linings' following Cyclone Narelle
text:
An outback cattle station and popular tourist stay has wrapped up a better-than-expected tourist season, seven months after Cyclone Narelle left it in ruins.

Bullara Station made headlines in March when destructive winds and flooding raged through the Exmouth Gulf property, 1,200 kilometres north of Perth.

Station owner Edwina Shallcross said the cyclone "took us for six".

"We initially thought, 'This is amazing; we're actually going to get some decent rain,' so we were quite elated and joyous about it all, but then it quickly turned around, and we realised we were in a lot of trouble," she said.

'Everything went under'

Loading...

Ms Shallcross said they had experienced significant cyclones in the past, but Narelle was unprecedented.

They were left without clean water and power for weeks, and had to rebuild the station from scratch as more than two metres of floodwater rose across Bullara's 100,000 hectares.

"In terms of infrastructure, everywhere you looked, everything went under," she said.

"The cost to the business has been really extensive, and of course the emotional and physical pressures that come with something like it, it's been a lot."

Station owner Tim Shallcross paddleboards through Bullara Station. (Facebook: Bullara Station Stay)

Ms Shallcross said that, due to the team's hard work, they were able to open the station to tourists just weeks after the cyclone.

"We're so grateful and proud of all our team; they've just stood by us and been really incredible," Ms Shallcross said.

Bullara welcomed back tourists just weeks after Cyclone Narelle tore through the property. (ABC Pilbara: Nikki Bailey)

The iconic red dirt and vast rangelands have made a comeback, but in the days following the cyclone, the station was unrecognisable.

Video footage showed livestock wading through neck-high water and smaller animals finding shelter in floating cars.

"I remember watching a cow reversing in towards the wind just outside my window and thinking, 'Gosh, they're amazing, just how they know to put their backs to the wind,' and it was just head down," Ms Shallcross said.

"It was quite fascinating; they just try and get near something quite solid and try to find some high ground; they're pretty switched on."

What appears to be a goat seeks shelter in a car while being pummelled with fast-moving flood water. (Facebook: Bullara Station Stay)

Silver linings

Seeing the damage to the infrastructure, Ms Shallcross was initially worried about how the station's livestock survived.

"Last week we finished trucking out our cattle, and the silver linings are those shiny healthy Droughtmasters," she said.

"They couldn't be in better condition and just the feed on the ground; it's so positive to see the country coming back again, so there's always a silver lining."

As the season came to a close earlier this month, Ms Shallcross bid farewell to the final tourists of the year and sent the last of the cattle off to market.

"We're looking forward to a bit of relaxing now, and hopefully we don't have to go through that again."

title: Judge finds Aboriginal protection order on goldmine 'fundamentally flawed'
text:
The Federal Court has found a fundamentally flawed decision-making process led to the granting of an Aboriginal protection order over part of a billion-dollar New South Wales goldmine project.

Justice James Stellios has published his redacted reasons for overturning an Aboriginal protection order applied to part of the McPhillamys goldmine site near Blayney.

Former environment minister Tanya Plibersek made the declaration under Section 10 of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Heritage Protection Act in August 2024.

It was granted to protect the headwaters and springs of the Belubula River, which is where the mine's tailings dam was to be built.

The proposed site of the tailings dam for the McPhillamys Gold Project near Blayney. (Supplied: Regis Resources)

The then-minister's decision was based on the blue-banded bee Dreaming story shared by Wiradjuri elders.

In his reasons, Justice Stellios concluded "the decision-making process was fundamentally flawed because of the failure to treat the revelation of the Blue Banded Bee Dreaming story as a new application".

Timing of new information

Justice Stellios's judgment does not centre on the merits of the protection applications, but rather the nature of certain information and the time it was received by the federal Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW).

When an application for Aboriginal protection is made, a government reporter or staff member is assigned to issue public notifications, consult interested individuals and organisations, assess the application and provide a report with recommendations to the minister.

The McPhillamys Gold Project received state and federal approval in March and May 2023, respectively.

Aboriginal elders provided details of the blue-banded bee Dreaming story in December 2023.

One of them asked for the story to be used to support a Section 10 application, and Justice Stellios noted the DCCEEW should have advised the minister that this request meant a new Section 10 application was required.

Tanya Plibersek made the declaration under Section 10 of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Heritage Protection Act in 2024. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

The judgment noted that the details of the blue-banded bee Dreaming story provided greater clarity about the particular significance of the area in question, which until then had been "identified at a high level of generality and in an unparticularised way".

Justice Stellios also noted that the Dreaming story was shared after the Section-10 report had been presented to the minister.

"While it was stated that the Minister considered the s 10 report, it should be evident at this stage that the revelation of the Blue Banded Bee Dreaming story occurred after that report was provided to the Minister," Justice Stellios's reasons said.

He concluded that the legally mandated government reporter process, which included public consultation, should have started "afresh".

"In my view, it could not be said that the public were given an effective opportunity to address the more specific and particular claim for protection, or that there was an adequate public ventilation of the particular significance of the application area or the threat posed to it," Justice Stellios's reasons stated.

The judgment noted that the DCCEEW considered the Dreaming story a "subset" of information already provided and that it did not warrant a new application.

Justice Stellios disagreed.

"The [government] reporter was denied the opportunity to consider representations on the particular significance of the application area and the Minister was, thereby, denied the opportunity to consider the reporter's report on that central and material matter," his reasons said.

Regis Resources contested the validity of the Aboriginal protection order in the Federal Court. (ABC News: Lani Oataway)

He noted that while recommencing the public consultation process would have led to additional costs and further delays, the minister could have nominated the same government reporter to consider the fresh application.

Justice Stellios ended by saying he was aware that his decision would mean a "further protracted" process for the application, which would now be referred back to the federal government for redetermination.

In a statement, a federal government spokesperson said the Albanese government remained committed to reforming the relevant legislation to "deliver more clarity and certainty to everyone involved".

Consultation on proposed legislative reforms is due to start before the end of the year.

title: Simmons says cruel injury ahead of NBA season 'not the end of my story'
text:
Ben Simmons's burgeoning NBA comeback has been halted after he suffered a torn Achilles during practice just days out from the season-opener.

The Australian had shown promising signs during the Sacramento Kings' pre-season contests after spending all of last season away from the NBA.

According to a Kings release, Simmons was injured during a live drill before an MRI scan revealed a torn right Achilles tendon. Simmons will undergo surgery.

The 30-year-old's career has been derailed by injuries over the past five years. Prior to his injury issues, Simmons made three NBA All-Star teams and was considered one of the best defensive players in the league.

Despite the setback, Simmons is adamant the injury does not spell an end to his NBA career.

"I've faced challenges before that tested me mentally, physically, and emotionally, and I've found a way through every single one of them," he wrote on Instagram.

"This injury is another chapter in my journey, not the end of my story.

"It's never easy being away from the game I love, especially after everything it took to get back here.

"But if there's one thing I've learned, it's that adversity doesn't define you. How you respond to it does.

"I've been knocked down before, and I've always found a way to get back up. This time will be no different."

Simmons signed a one-year deal with the Kings last month.

After playing 81 of 82 regular-season games in his rookie season, Simmons's durability has gradually waned.

He has not played in excess of 60 regular season games since the 2018-19 season, and he managed just 50 in his most recent NBA season with the Brooklyn Nets and LA Clippers in 2024-25.

Simmons recently detailed his career and his comeback attempt in an ESPN documentary where he hit back at critics who have questioned his love for basketball.

"Everyone has their thing that they love and they have passion for, and basketball is that passion for me," he said.

"All these people talk about I don't love the game. That's bullshit.

"I've played through the injuries. I've broken my foot, I've rehabbed, I've had multiple back surgeries. I've been through it all.

"If I didn't love the game, trust me, I would be at home, I'd be fishing … but I love this shit."

The NBA regular season kicks off on Wednesday morning AEDT when the Detroit Pistons host the Boston Celtics. Sacramento's season opener takes place in Los Angeles against the Clippers on Thursday afternoon.

title: Victorian Liberal Nationals promise to return V/Line trains to Mildura and Horsham
text:
The Victorian Liberal National Coalition has promised to bring passenger train services back to Mildura for the first time in more than 30 years, if it wins the state election.

V/Line train services between Melbourne and Mildura were axed in 1993 by the former Liberal premier Jeff Kennett.

The Coalition said passenger services would return to Mildura and Dimboola by mid-2029 as part of its $51.2 million Wimmera Mallee Rail plan.

The Mildura train service would stop at Red Cliffs, Ouyen, Birchip, Donald, St Arnaud and Dunolly before connecting with Melbourne-bound trains at Maryborough.

The Dimboola service would stop at Horsham, Murtoa and Stawell, before connecting with the wider train network at Ararat.

The former Kennett Liberal government axed Mildura's train service 33 years ago. (ABC News: Wade Stephens)

The Coalition said there would be three return services a week on each corridor.

Decades-long campaign

Mildura remains the largest regional city in the state without access to a passenger rail service.

Currently, the nearest passenger train service is based in Swan Hill, two and a half hours away, with passengers required to catch a coach service from Mildura to Swan Hill.

Alternatively, residents can take the overnight bus to Melbourne, but both options take about eight hours each way.

Passengers wait at the Mildura bus station, hoping to get a seat on a 3:55am coach to Swan Hill.

Liberal leader Jess Wilson said bringing back passenger rail would give people across the Wimmera and Mallee a more affordable way to travel and stay connected to the rest of Victoria.

Community welcomes decision

Rail Revival Alliance president Noel Laidlaw has been advocating for the Mildura service and was "delighted" to be heard by one of the major parties.

He said passenger rail was particularly needed for people who could not afford to fly, and those who were not able to, or did not want to, drive.

"There are always alternatives but they're always the second best," he said.

"There's nothing like getting on the train, sitting back and getting to your destination."

Nhill resident Margaret Millington had also been advocating for the return of passenger rail to the Wimmera for nearly a decade.

She said getting it back would be "a life changer".

"People need that infrastructure to connect and just to survive," she said.

"I know a lot of the Karen [community], I know a lot of sick people who are travelling up and down, it's going to make a world of difference if it comes to fruition."

Margaret Millington is one of many Wimmera residents calling for the return of a passenger service. (ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya)

Member for Mildura Jade Benham said the commitment had been a "long time coming".

"Twenty-one of the last 25 years have been under Labor, and anytime the question has been asked if [Labor has] any intention of reinstating the train, the answer has been unequivocally no," she said.

"My job as the local member is to listen to the community, and we are bringing back the Mildura train."

The Victorian Coalition has pledged $51.2 million towards the Wimmera Mallee Rail plan. (ABC News: Sarah Buchecker)

Labor criticises plan costings

When asked if Labor would match the commitment, a spokesperson said the Coalition's costings were "flat-out wrong".

"Line upgrades cost anywhere from almost $200 million to more than $500 million — we know this because we have upgraded every regional passenger train line," the Labor spokesperson said.

"The Liberals shut down the train to Mildura and can't be trusted to bring it back again."

In response, the Coalition said the initial $51.2 million investment would fund infrastructure improvements, potential train acquisition and refurbishment, and operating costs over four years.

In 2010, a government-commissioned report estimated the cost to return the passenger service was about $500 million, although that plan included large-scale upgrades to tracks and brand new stations.

The Coalition said the new estimate took into account track upgrades that had already occurred as part of the Murray Basin Rail Project, among other adjustments.

Australia’s largest listed data centre developer has warned investors that power supply delays, likely caused by community opposition, will hit the development of its flagship West Footscray facility. Data centre giant NextDC sought a trading halt in its ASX-listed shares on Monday telling investors it needed to assess the impact of the delay in getting power to its M3 data centre in West Footscray. NextDC’s M3 data centre in West Footscray, Melbourne, in March this year. Joe Armao The company did not give a reason for the delay but analysts tipped it was likely the result of a fierce community blockade in Melbourne’s inner-west last month that brought a multi-million-dollar power pole expansion by electricity distributor Jemena to a standstill. Citigroup analyst Siraj Ahmed said in a briefing to investors that the trading halt likely related to electricity distributor Jemena’s pause on that project.

NextDC’s market admission is the clearest evidence yet that Victoria’s rapid push to attract power-hungry artificial intelligence infrastructure has run directly into grid constraints and suburban resistance. The M3 facility in West Footscray is designed to eventually span 10 hectares across an industrial pocket directly adjacent to residential homes. The data centre already takes up five hectares and is undergoing a $750 million expansion. But feeding the site required network operator Jemena to replace standard wooden electricity poles with 15-metre-high concrete structures carrying 66,000 volts down residential streets in West Footscray and neighbouring Yarraville.

Neither Jemena nor NextDC has confirmed the rollout was directly linked to the power pole pause. That rollout ground to a halt in Yarraville last month following direct action by local residents, who blockaded contractor trucks with parked cars, ignored door-knocks, and filled excavation pits to stop the high-voltage lines reaching the NextDC site. Then-premier Jacinta Allan with NextDC chief executive Craig Scroggie in 2025 in one of the data centre’s Melbourne premises. Justin McManus Jemena bowed to the pressure and has since paused work in Yarraville to allow for consultation, leaving the high-capacity power route unfinished. Many of the West Footscray power poles designed to carry the far higher voltage had already been installed. In its letter to the ASX, signed by NextDC company secretary Michael Helmer, the company said its board had not yet met to consider the full implications of the power delay. The trading halt will remain in place until Wednesday or until a full announcement is made.

Investigations 15-metre power poles started to pop up in inner Melbourne. However, the rapid influx of data halls occurred without corresponding planning by the Victorian state for the massive transmission upgrades required to power them. And, like in the US, community opposition to the mega-computer halls has risen.

Data centres consume about 2 per cent of national grid power, but the Australian Energy Market Operator projects that share could rise to 9 per cent by 2035 as AI adoption accelerates. Carroll last month brought in new rules on data centres to address growing community concerns. Accelerate Resources has unearthed high-grade manganese rock chips grading as much as 59.6 per cent and identified a completely new discovery at its Woodie Woodie North project in Western Australia’s prolific East Pilbara region. The results from the Faris and the freshly-minted Sea Turtle prospects have lit up a 12-kilometre-long mineralised corridor that has astonishingly only ever been tested by very shallow holes drilled 30 years ago. The discovery comes at a time when both government and industry are paying closer attention to securing manganese supply chains. Outcropping high-grade manganese at Accelerate Resources’ Woodie Woodie North project, just 55km north of Consolidated Minerals’ long-running Woodie Woodie manganese mine in the Pilbara. Surface sampling at the Faris prospect bagged a suite of impressive assays, with four rock chips grading between a hefty 53.9 per cent and a cracking 59.6 per cent manganese. Notably, the high-grade outcrop at Faris, just two kilometres south-east of the company’s Area 42 deposit, sits directly above shallow, historic drilling that delivered high-grade hits of 11m running 28.4 per cent manganese from just one-metre downhole and 3m assaying 39.1 per cent manganese from surface.

Mapping has defined a large iron and manganese alteration system measuring 650m by 400m that has previously never been drill tested. Rock chips from two new outcrops returned grades up to 31.4 per cent manganese, confirming the system is fertile. Accelerate Resources chief executive officer Luke Meter said: “The ongoing discovery of high-grade manganese along this exciting 12km trend continues to support the continuity of mineralisation through this extensive belt. At Sea Turtle, our geology team has found two new manganese outcrops inside a large alteration system that has not previously been drilled.” The new discoveries form part of a systematic exploration push and follow the company’s savvy move last month to consolidate 100 per cent ownership of the Woodie Woodie North project, clearing the decks of all legacy payments and royalties. The scrip-based deal means the company can now capture all the upside from these and any other new discoveries. Management says the simplified structure will also better support any potential funding, offtake or partnering discussions down the track. The Woodie Woodie North project sits 55km north of Consolidated Minerals’ long-running Woodie Woodie manganese mine and already hosts a maiden inferred mineral resource of 1.2 million tonnes grading 19.1 per cent manganese. That resource lies alongside a hefty exploration target of between 5.3 and 10.7 million tonnes (Mt) at grades of 10 to 19 per cent manganese.

Being on the doorstep of a major, multi-decade mining operation is an enviable position for any explorer. Accelerate is also actively de-risking the development pathway for its cornerstone Area 42 deposit, which holds a resource of 0.7Mt at 20.7 per cent manganese. Senator Jacqui Lambie (right), pictured with Pauline Hanson in the Senate, is the latest target in One Nation’s Please Explain cartoons. The Minns government will intervene to give a Hunter Valley coal mine a licence to dig up millions of tonnes more each year despite a seismic High Court ruling that found its approval was invalid because it had failed to reckon with emissions from Australian coal burnt overseas. Premier Chris Minns announced on Monday that the NSW government would step in to give MACH Energy legislated approval to increase production at the Mount Pleasant coal mine to 16.5 million tonnes a year, from its current limit of 12.5 million tonnes, until 2032. The Minns government has intervened to give MACH Energy’s Mount Pleasant Coal Mine Operations near Muswellbrook an expanded approval. Kate Geraghty Minns said the decision came after MACH Energy told the government it was preparing to sack half its workforce – about 400 people – before Christmas if its approval was not expanded. In return for boosting the mine’s annual production limit, the government said the company had agreed to sign a jobs guarantee that would establish a legal obligation to maintain staffing levels. The intervention comes after the High Court ruled a fortnight ago that a 2022 approval by the NSW Independent Planning Commission was invalid because it had failed to properly consider the climate impact of coal exported overseas from the mine.

Advertisement

The ruling – which found the IPC had not properly considered the impact of so-called “scope 3 emissions” – led to immediate calls from the Coalition and One Nation for Labor to urgently pass new laws overruling the High Court. Related Article Updated

High Court of Australia ‘Pandora’s box’: High Court decision could reopen coal mine approval cases Despite initially playing down the need for legal change, Minns said Indonesian billionaire Anthoni Salim’s MACH Energy informed the government it was preparing to sack the workers before Christmas. That was because it had scaled up its workforce to prepare for the increase in its production limit to 21 million tonnes a year as approved by the IPC. “These are not easy decisions,” Minns said. “They’re incredibly difficult, and I’ve agonised over this one. “The truth of the matter is there’s some people who say that the only thing to worry about is industry and jobs in all and every circumstance, and there are others who say you should only be worrying about the environment in any and all circumstances … we have to do both.

Advertisement

“We have to approach these things in a commonsense way and draw conclusions so that we’re making progress towards our climate goals, while at the same time not tipping hundreds and hundreds of families onto the scrap heap weeks before Christmas.” NSW Natural Resources Minister Courtney Houssos said the new legislation – which will be introduced during the next sitting fortnight – would include requirements to limit scope 3 emissions in line with the IPC’s recent Hunter Valley Operations mine approval. It means that, in effect, the company can only export coal to countries that are signatories to the Paris climate agreement. The decision prompted immediate backlash from environmental groups, which accused the government of interfering with independent planning rules. Greens MP Sue Higginson said Labor had capitulated to “threats and taken the side of the billionaire coal company over the community”. “This is an incredible new low for the Minns Labor government, bypassing the planning process and the law as laid down by the High Court of Australia,” she said. “One thing is clear, under Labor the coal mining giants are writing the laws, and they are laws that will cause significant unassessed climate pollution and hurt communities.”

Advertisement

Lock the Gate national co-ordinator Georgina Woods called it “cynical and dangerous political interference in the planning system”, accusing Labor of “manufacturing a crisis to give special treatment to a coal company”. Related Article Climate policy ‘Triply nervous’: Massive coal mine braced for challenge after High Court ruling “There is no threat to jobs at Mount Pleasant, which already has approval to stay open for another six years,” she said. Labor is facing significant pressure from One Nation in the Hunter Valley. Asked if his government would have made the same decision if an election was not looming, Minns said: “I believe we would have. “What I would say in relation to that very fair question is: Look at the government’s record over the last six months,” he said, referring to a series of manufacturing announcements in the Hunter valley and the Tomago Aluminium bailout.

“We’re a Labor government. We do need to protect jobs.” Minns denied the government was undermining rules around the independent assessment of mines, saying the impact of the High Court judgment on MACH Energy’s expansion would still need to be worked out in the lower courts. He called it a “partial approval to keep pace with the current workforce that’s on the ground in that community”. “It’s a difficult decision to make,” he said. “In normal circumstances, you wouldn’t want to do it. You’d want the court to make the decision before any expansion or a decision from the company. Great Southern Mining has hit paydirt with maiden reverse circulation (RC) drilling at its Amy Clarke prospect within the Duketon gold project near Laverton in Western Australia, intersecting high-grade gold along a previously defined 4.7-kilometre mineralised corridor. The company says the results reinforce the prospect’s potential, sitting just 12km from Regis Resources’ Garden Well processing facility. The 18-hole, 2248-metre campaign tested higher-grade zones identified by earlier aircore drilling. It appears to have done its job, returning a clutch of impressive near-surface intercepts along strike and at depth, extending mineralisation down-dip by up to 50m and broadening areas of higher-grade gold. Reverse circulation drilling at Great Southern Mining’s Amy Clarke prospect within the Duketon Gold Project in Western Australia. The headline result came from a hole that delivered 5m grading 6.71 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 51m, including a richer three-metre core going 10.4g/t gold. Other notable hits likely to make management smile included 2m at 8.92g/t within a broader 11-metre interval grading 1.86g/t gold from 45m. A third returned multiple mineralised zones, the best of which was 8m at 1.44g/t from 67m, featuring 2m at 4.7g/t gold.

Advertisement

‘Amy Clarke is an emerging discovery with immense upside. The gold starts from surface and continues to the extent of the drilling in the fresh rock.’ Great Southern Mining managing director Matthew Keane Further results show the system’s breadth, with intercepts of 5m at 1.81g/t gold from 61m, 2m at 1.41g/t from a very shallow 7m and multiple one-metre slices grading more than 2g/t gold. Reported intervals are downhole lengths, with true widths not yet confirmed. The company says while drilling remains shallow, averaging less than 100m below surface, with mineralisation observed from surface in the oxidised, or weathered, horizon and extending at depth into fresh rock. Geologically, the gold at Amy Clarke is associated with quartz veining and disseminated or coarse pyrite. According to Great Southern, the prospect lies in a high-strain structural corridor, generally near contacts between different rock types, with the structures currently modelled as steeply east-dipping, a classic setting for gold deposition in the Eastern Goldfields. Great Southern managing director Matthew Keane said: “The Company’s aggressive 2026 RC drilling campaign has delivered strong results across three key targets, incorporating Amy Clarke, the Golden Boulder discovery and Mon Ami, with all three returning high-grade intercepts and material extensions to known mineralisation.”

Advertisement

With a successful maiden RC campaign in the bag, detailed geological and structural mapping is underway, alongside multi-element geochemistry of selected intervals, to better understand the controls on mineralisation and home in on the highest-grade zones. Great Southern says it has already started planning for the next phase, likely to include follow-up RC drilling and potential diamond drilling. Initial drilling is expected to focus on open lodes in the northern part of Amy Clarke and the central section of the 4.7-kilometre trend. The system remains open to the south, where little drilling has been undertaken beyond the company’s southernmost holes, leaving a substantial stretch of prospective ground largely untested. The latest results add another string to Great Southern’s bow at Duketon, complementing its nearby Golden Boulder discovery, where historic production averaged an eye-watering grade of 28.6g/t gold and the company has since outlined mineralisation along 3.5km of strike. The junior explorer is awaiting assays from another 6000m of ongoing drilling at the southern end of Golden Boulder and the Golden Boulder East trend, 3km southwest of Amy Clarke. Amy Clarke is interpreted to lie along the same structural trend that hosts Regis’ Erlistoun open pit mine, about 3km to the north, which contains a 320,000-ounce resource grading 1.9g/t gold. The Garden Well processing facility, with a capacity of five million tonnes per annum, is 12km to the northeast. The broader Duketon Greenstone Belt is no stranger to big gold discoveries, with mining heavyweight Regis Resources identifying more than eight million ounces of gold resources across the region. Great Southern’s tenure includes significant sections of the major shear zones that are known to host the majority of the deposits across the belt.

Advertisement

In a gold-rich neighbourhood where proximity to processing infrastructure can be worth its weight in gold, Great Southern is assembling an increasingly enticing collection of prospects on the doorstep of established mining operations. With Amy Clarke shaping up as another potential discovery and a swag of fresh assays from Golden Boulder still to come, the company’s Duketon gold story looks to have plenty more chapters left to write. title: Tame Impala’s spectacular show a kaleidoscope of colour and controlled chaos
text:
Advertisement

Key points MUSIC: Tame Impala puts on a colour and laser-filled show at Rod Laver Arena

JAZZ: The Melbourne International Jazz Festival has kicked off for 2026

OPERA: Opera Australia returns to the State Theatre with The Wagner Gala Concert

MUSIC: Mozart, Salieri and Pleyel shows the Australian Brandenburg Orchestra at its best

DANCE: Lucy Guerin returns to the stage with Place Dances

MUSIC

Tame Impala ★★★★

Rod Laver Arena, October 14 Kevin Parker loves a laser. In a 2015 Rolling Stone interview with the Tame Impala doyen, it’s revealed that a bedroom in his Fremantle home – the same house in which he’s then just self-made his brilliant third LP Currents – is filled with dozens of automated stage lights on stands. Parker explains that instead of complaining about a light show he’s not happy with, he decided to teach himself how to design his own. Kevin Parker’s meticulousness is all over the spectacular Tame Impala live experience. Richard Clifford Checks out. Parker’s meticulousness is all over the spectacular Tame Impala live experience. While he presents as the chill savant who’s wandered onto the spaceship stage at the rave, armed with a casual jumper, floppy hair and a selection of monster hits etched into the universal songbook, an enormous rig of tessellated lights and lasers unfolds in increasingly eye-boggling configurations. It all makes the springy house chords of Breathe Deeper, arena-singalong melody of Feels Like I Only Go Backwards, and mirror-maze of groove feints that propel guitar stomper Elephant feel like the apex of the live music experience. A bedroom producer’s fantasy in full flight.

Advertisement

Grittier electronic tracks from new LP Deadbeat are offset by the sweet tenor of Parker’s voice. Dracula and Afterthought – both with nods to Michael Jackson’s Thriller – are fun highlights, Parker stepping off-stage in pop star mode to slap hands with fans. The squealing crowd skews much younger than the 40-year-old Parker, suggesting his arc from airy psych-rock into a signature DIY-brand of mainstream pop has energised new generations of fans. Parker’s spectacular Rod Laver Arena show is a bedroom producer’s fantasy in full flight. Richard Clifford Mid-set, Parker ambles backstage, followed by a cameraman who films him appearing to urinate in a bathroom. He re-emerges by the mixing desk on a lamp-lit stage to sip from a can of Melbourne Bitter and sing insular Deadbeat tracks Ethereal Connection and Not My World, surrounded by 14,000 people waving phone torches. In the shadows, his longtime band chug away in service to a set list that rarely changes and a frontman who lets his lasers do the talking. Where I’m sitting, the sound mix is overwhelmed by shuddering bass frequencies – a disappointment for enjoying the production of a famously meticulous sound nerd. But the annoyance fades as we cascade into mass singalongs Let It Happen, Eventually, and The Less I Know the Better, each exploding with a kaleidoscope of confetti, colour and controlled chaos around this clever Peter Pan from Perth at the centre of it all.

Reviewed by Marcus Teague

Advertisement

JAZZ

Melbourne International Jazz Festival

Opening weekend, October 16-18 The opening weekend of the Melbourne International Jazz Festival was overflowing with premieres, festival commissions and first-time collaborations. Joey Alexander (left) performs alongside Young Monk and Skylar Tang (trumpet). Duncographic In Friday night’s double bill at the Recital Centre (curated in partnership with New York’s Jazz at Lincoln Center), the phenomenal Indonesian pianist Joey Alexander fronted two separate ensembles. The first was an international iteration of Young Monk, a jazz project in which rising stars of the future interpret the music of Thelonious Monk. Here, Alexander and the superb New York-based trumpeter Skylar Tang were joined by three gifted Melbourne players.

Advertisement

Alexander and Tang both spoke earnestly and eloquently about their love of Monk’s music, and their passion radiated from the stage as they played. Local players Toby Barrett, Lily Appelt and Ebs Daramola clearly relished the opportunity to perform with international peers on a festival stage, and the whole ensemble buzzed with energy and vitality. Xani Kolac performs at the festival. Max Roux The second half featured Alexander with his eponymous ensemble, which allowed the pianist to shine in a set of exuberant originals. Yes, the preternatural virtuosity that brought him to the world’s attention when he was still a child was on dazzling display. But the rhapsodic cascades that poured from the 23-year-old’s hands never came across as empty showmanship. On the contrary, each sparkling melodic extension, harmonic exploration or spirited interaction with his bandmates felt like a natural expression of an artist doing what he was born to do, with irrepressible joy and unshakeable conviction. On Saturday, the New York-based Cuban saxophonist Yosvany Terry led another specially assembled outfit alongside his brother, bassist Yunior Terry (now based in Melbourne), US pianist Brett Williams and drummer Julian Miltenberger. Together, they formed a marvellously potent and muscular ensemble – at times urgent and propulsive, at times breezily buoyant. The final tune (Summer Relief) featured Yosvany on shekere, summoning Afro-Cuban deities with intricate rhythms and invocatory chants before inviting the band – and the audience – to join him in this contemporary reinvention of ancient rituals. Later that night, electric violinist and composer Xani Kolac premiered a compelling new suite, Kołacz, at Howler in Brunswick. Kolac is the festival’s Take Note artist for 2026, and used her commission to delve into her Polish heritage and create a deeply personal work exploring her search for identity and belonging.

Advertisement

As she explained from the stage, this search also encompassed her quest for acceptance as an artist whose music refuses to be bound by genre. It eventually became a celebration of her distinctive creative voice. Using violin, accordion (played by Tuulikki Bartosik), bass, drums, vocals and an array of pedals and effects, her quartet conjured a constantly changing sound world incorporating folk-like whimsy, experimental rock, abstract sound art and boisterous East European dance. Sunday brought another premiere: Eugene Ball’s Continuum, commissioned by ABC Jazz to celebrate the 50th anniversary of Jazztrack. Designed to reflect the impact and legacy of this long-running national radio program, Ball’s masterfully written and beautifully realised suite featured an eight-piece ensemble gliding across stately big-band-style tunes, strutting with jaunty classic-jazz vigour, bristling with angular precision and plunging into pools of bold, free-form drama. The Shai Maestro Trip perform at Chapel Off Chapel. Max Roux Then came the Shai Maestro Trio’s sublime performance at Chapel Off Chapel. This was not a premiere or a new collaboration (though singer Gian Slater joined the band as a guest for one exquisite tune, Gloria). It was, however, the most heart-swelling, spirit-lifting encounter you could imagine. The chapel’s illuminated stained-glass windows provided an appropriate backdrop for this music, which had a luminous and often transportive quality. Using intuition as their guide, Maestro and his supremely empathetic bandmates (Reuben Rogers on bass and Ofri Nehemya on drums) built jewel-like melodies into soulfully ecstatic grooves or flamenco-fuelled climaxes as they swelled and surged in restless waves, sweeping the audience into their orbit and holding us utterly spellbound.

Reviewed by Jessica Nicholas

The Melbourne International Jazz Festival continues until Sunday

NOTE: No star rating has been applied to the above review
