OPERA

The Wagner Gala Concert ★

Opera Australia, Ian Potter State Theatre, October 16 The State Theatre has only been closed for about 2½ years, but to Melbourne’s opera community, it’s felt like an age. Orchestra Victoria performs Opera Australia’s Wagner Gala on October 16. Jeff Busby The national opera company has been something of a wand’ring minstrel in that time, turning up at The Regent Theatre and Hamer Hall, before making a short-lived sojourn to Margaret Court Arena, where its 2024 production of Tosca went out in straight sets. OA sought to make a triumphant return to the newly named Ian Potter State Theatre with an all-Wagner gala. For something so long in the making, it was frustratingly underdeveloped.

Advertisement

Orchestra Victoria did its diligent best, but it felt as though the players and German conductor Michael Güttler had just met that morning – most musicians barely looked up from their scores at him, and some looked sullen. Güttler made strident gestures at them in return, the resultant interpretations of the many overtures and preludes a torrent of Wagnerian generality. This is music that should stir the soul. It was fine. Editor's pick Live music Baker Boy showered with gifts by young fans at milestone gig English soprano Catherine Foster was merely going through the motions, Russian tenor Sergey Skorokhodov was clearly unwell and coughing so frequently it appeared doubtful he would make it through his final aria. Australian baritone James Clayton had the least to do but was the most commendable. This program felt a million miles away from a party. We were meant to be celebrating opera being back in this beautiful theatre, so why was this whole affair so sombre? This gala was not opera for the people. The absence of surtitles made an already forbidding program needlessly inaccessible. Most of the audience were left to decipher some big German feelings, delivered by a mostly international cast, and wonder what it’s all got to do with the city of Melbourne and the reopening of our beloved theatre. This program did not meet the moment, and fell far short of what patient, passionate Melburnians deserve.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies

Advertisement

MUSIC

Mozart, Salieri and Pleyel ★★★★

Australian Brandenburg Orchestra, Melbourne Recital Centre, October 17 Billed as “a classical powerhouse”, this program of works by Mozart, Salieri and Ignaz Pleyel sets up an interesting three-way conversation between three accomplished but contrasting contemporaries. Artistic director Paul Dyer conducts from the fortepiano. Laura Manariti Contrary to popular belief, Salieri was an actual admirer of Mozart. However, the Sinfonia from his “heroic-comic” opera Cublai, gran Kan de Tartari (ostensibly based on the life of Kublai Khan) was more reminiscent of Beethoven with its muscular treatment of the predominant triadic material. Mozart’s Divertimento for Stings in D major, K. 136 was given sprightly treatment; broad brushstrokes emphasising its elegantly tapered arcs of melody enhanced by the soft-grained timbre of the period string band.

Advertisement

Only recently attributed to him, Pleyel’s Concerto for Violone in E-flat major is receiving its world premiere performances on this tour by the Australian Brandenburg Orchestra with its own principal bass Robert Nairn as soloist. A precursor of the double bass, the violone has five strings instead of four. This substantial work shows the influence of Pleyel’s teacher Haydn, with its deftly variegated approach to orchestration and rhythm. Nairn rose with aplomb to the concerto’s various technical challenges, not least to playing for the most part in the instrument’s upper register where accurate intonation and well-projected resonance can be harder to achieve. A novel second-movement pizzicato cadenza offset the dramatic “storm and stress” style of the outer movements. A precursor of the double bass, the violone has five strings instead of four. Laura Manariti The dynamo in this powerhouse was undoubtedly Mozart’s Symphony No. 39 in E-flat major, K. 543. Conducted by artistic director Paul Dyer from the fortepiano, this passionately committed account was notable for its elegant poise, balancing moments of rhetorical drama with well-judged wit and bringing to the fore the interplay between the well-coloured strings, wind and brass. Undergirded by buoyant rhythms and razor-sharp passage work, leading to a sudden conclusion, this was the Brandenburg at its brilliant best.

Reviewed by Tony Way

Advertisement

DANCE

Place Dances ★★★★

Buxton Contemporary, Southbank, until October 18 This fascinating new solo work marks a significant return for Lucy Guerin. She largely stopped performing in her own work after launching her company some 25 years ago. Now, as she steps away from that company, she once again steps into the limelight. Place Dances by Lucy Guerin at Buxton Contemporary. Gianna Rizzo It’s a long absence but the interval seems to collapse when she appears: the same quiet, compact, unflappable presence. The same sharp profile and cool expression. The practice of creating and thinking through her body has plainly endured. This is part dance and part lecture, with Guerin tracing the sources of her creativity. Her spoken reflections are presented in an adjoining room, but the sound carries into the main space, as though lecture and dance were neighbouring exhibits.

Advertisement

The dance is like a distillation of her essential impulses as a choreographer: quick, deft gestures, short steps, upright posture and active fingers. The organisation of the space, too, lays bare her tendency to enclose the space, to make stages within the stage. It’s an intriguing companion to NEWRETRO, her expansive 2023 reflection on her work with Lucy Guerin Inc. Both inhabit galleries with austere black-and-white presentations. But this is darker – the act of recollection exposes the doubts that accompany her desires. Guerin’s interest in dialogues between incompatible ideas finds expression in the alternation of lecture and dance. Then, in the middle of the work, there’s a literal dialogue with herself. It’s a conceit that perhaps only her quiet earnestness could make persuasive. For Guerin, imagination is central: the ability to conceive not simply how a body might move, but where. To imagine a body placed in another world, moving through another atmosphere, is the origin of her choreographic endeavours. Crafted with characteristic dramaturgical care, Place Dances offers candid, almost ingenuous reflections on artistic motivations. There are glimpses of gothic melancholy, but it feels like an exciting beginning: a transition with the promise of dances still to come.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann

Advertisement

MUSIC

Macy Gray ★★★

The Encore Tour

Hamer Hall, October 13 Someone in the crowd calls out “Macy!” – another yells “Where are you?” The crowd is getting impatient by this point, starting to clap to entice Macy Gray on to the stage. It’s understandable, given they’ve been waiting for more than an hour, including a 15-minute late start to the event and a dynamic performance from support act Emi Secrest. Macy Gray performs at Melbourne’s Hamer Hall. Martin Philbey Eventually the band walks out, all of them wearing a similar afro wig (perhaps it’s a nod to her signature hair?). Gray finally strolls on stage in a bright orange summer dress and red fingerless gloves, launching into her signature raspy tones to cheers. Gray returns to Australia following a successful 2024 run that celebrated the 25th anniversary of her debut album, On How Life Is. The 2026 The Encore Tour is even more expansive, covering metro and regional venues nationally.

Advertisement

Related Article Take 7 Macy Gray was dumped by her record label while pregnant. Then her career really took off Tuesday’s show was a postponed session from September 11 due to a 24-hour strike by Arts Centre Melbourne staff. Instead of a soulful evening of live music, the public were met with a picket line and public rally. (The industrial dispute has since been resolved after staff accepted an improved pay offer.) The cancelled performance didn’t seem to faze Gray, as she made no mention of it. She continued to swish her skirt, side step and clap her hands to the funky beat. She encouraged the audience to sing and dance along, stating “this ain’t no library”. She reiterates to the audience that she and the band have come all the way from Los Angeles “to hear you sing to us”. Gray with members of her band, who bring a more jazz-inspired approach to her original songs, on stage at Hamer Hall. Martin Philbey The band brings a more jazz-inspired approach to her original tracks, including shifting up the island groove in Witness. She changes the lyrics, encouraging the audience to repeat “and I wish I was Jesus” followed by “I’ll fix it for ya”.

Advertisement

Alongside other originals, such as I’ve Committed Murder, she sings covers of Radiohead’s Creep, Boney M.’s Sunny and Fred Said Right’s I’m Too Sexy. A disgruntled couple leaves early, complaining that they didn’t pay to hear cover songs. The set finishes at 10.50pm – late for a school night. But Gray doesn’t leave without singing her most well-known song, I Try, which gets fans to their feet, and joining in the chorus.

Reviewed by Vyshnavee Wijekumar DANCE

The Sleeping Beauty ★★★★

Regent Theatre, until October 18 The Stuttgart Ballet is in town, offering a rare chance to see a major European company dance one of its signature storybook ballets – with all the old-world charm and seriousness you could want. It’s also a chance to see a handful of genuine international ballet stars. First among them is Elisa Badenes, who danced Aurora on opening night, a dancer with exceptional composure and the silkiest of turns. The Stuttgart Ballet is in town. Kate Longley

Advertisement

Her Prince Désiré was Henrik Erikson: neat as a folded napkin in everything he does. His partnering with Badenes was compelling throughout, culminating in an exquisite grand pas de deux during the marriage festivities. The highlight was a diagonal of supported turns and plunging fish dives where, for one blissful moment, the two dancers appeared so connected, so entirely at one, that it was unclear who was supporting who. The wicked fairy Carabosse was danced by Jason Reilly, a veteran dramatic dynamo. He has a distinctive presence: quick, harassed, mocking, but earnest even when parodying the classical steps of the others. Carabosse has an elevated significance in Marcia Haydée’s version of the ballet. Haydée has transformed the contest between Carabosse and the Lilac Fairy into a sort of epic contest between good and evil. It can seem a little absurd – too much drama for the fey conceit – but this is a production that is very much of its time. Created in 1987, it’s essentially a Cold War fairy tale, showing a world dominated by two great powers. Mizuki Amemiya of The Stuttgart Ballet. Kate Longley

Advertisement

Abigail Willson-Heisel brought unflappable presence to the Lilac Fairy, while among the other dancers, Riccardo Ferlito drew the eye with the height and energy of his leaps as the bare-chested Ali Baba. It’s a long way to travel just to perform The Sleeping Beauty, even if it is a defining production. Once upon a time, they might have brought a second ballet to show another side of their repertoire. But visits by international companies of this stature – any stature, really – are few and far between these days.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann MUSIC

Isata Kanneh-Mason ★★★★

Melbourne Recital Centre, October 9 Navigating a journey from darkness to light, pianist Isata Kanneh-Mason’s Australian debut recital offered plenty of familiar music. Bookended by two of Beethoven’s most popular sonatas, the “Moonlight” and the “Waldstein”, it also included Ravel’s astoundingly imaginative but fiendishly difficult Gaspard de la nuit. Two works by Bulgarian-English composer Dobrinka Tabakova provided a contrasting contemporary aesthetic. Isata Kanneh-Mason performs at Melbourne Recital Centre on October 9, 2026 Laura Manariti

Advertisement

In Beethoven’s famous moonlit opening, Kanneh-Mason’s striking ability for extremely restrained dynamics and tone colour might have suggested a burgeoning sense of drama, yet this remained unrealised. The blazing finale displayed her prodigious technique, even if greater detail could have been revealed with lighter pedalling. Editor's pick Melbourne live reviews Jealousy, friendship and love take centre-stage in this story In Ravel’s brightly hued triptych, the water sprite Ondine splashed around in a luxurious aqueous soundscape while Kanneh-Mason’s trademark restraint lent the scene of the scaffold appropriate eeriness. She also convincingly captured Scarbo’s caprice, mischief and malevolence. After a symbolic change from dark evening gown to shorter pale blue dress, Kanneh-Mason turned to two works by Tabakova, containing the nucleus of the program. Nocturne, an attractive minimalist miniature summoned up night. Using harmonics and repeated notes, Halo effectively evoked a lunar halo which becomes increasingly bright. Clearly close to her heart, Kanneh-Mason played the “Waldstein” with great devotion, ensuring that the finale’s beginning did point to the dawn (an alternative nickname for the work). The blazing sunshine of the closing pages, however, were clouded over by some heavy pedalling.

Advertisement

Impressive as Kanneh-Mason’s playing is, trading some technical brilliance for a wider tonal palette and greater emotional abandon would have taken the performance to a higher level. An over-the-top arrangement of the 1960s hit I Say a Little Prayer for You provided a buoyant encore for the enthusiastic audience.

Reviewed by Tony Way MUSIC

Pekka Kuusisto: Legends and Luminaries ★★★★

Australian Chamber Orchestra, Melbourne Recital Centre, October 10 Ebullience is at the heart of Pekka Kuusisto’s artistic DNA. Joy, passion, commitment and a sense of fun are among the enviable qualities the Finnish violinist and composer brought to his latest collaboration with the Australian Chamber Orchestra. Pekka Kuusisto (left) performs with the Australian Chamber Orchestra. Nic Walker

Advertisement

As guest leader, Kuusisto helmed the orchestra through a program of contrasting styles, all with their own aural appeal. In Kuusisto’s thoughtful arrangement of excerpts from Mozart’s The Magic Flute, a little messiness was the price paid for an overture that ran at bullet train speed. Once the high-octane excitement subsided, beautifully shaped lyrical moments emerged before leading into the Queen of the Night’s aria. Editor's pick Melbourne Fringe Festival Not just red noses and creepy characters: Why it’s time to give clowning another chance Written for Kuusisto and premiered with the ACO Collective in 2019, American composer Nico Muhly’s Shrink: Concerto for Violin and Strings is a tour de force that is a perfect fit for the dedicatee’s mercurial personality. Across the work’s 22 minutes, Muhly weaves an intricate, compelling tapestry of textures, while the soloist jumps through every technical hoop imaginable. Kuusisto clearly thrives on such challenges, bringing unflagging zeal and a wealth of colour and emotion to the cleverly constructed score that exploits narrowing intervals alluded to in the title. Receiving its first Australian performances on this tour, Pulitzer Prize-winning composer Ellen Reid’s “paean to the Californian landscape”, West Coast Sky Eternal elicited an empathetic performance. Its shifting textural perspectives are intriguing at first before an extended pizzicato passage tends to unbalance its structure.

Advertisement

Clearly revelling in Kuusisto’s leadership, an arrangement of Mendelssohn’s String Quintet No. 2 in B-flat, Op. 87 received classic ACO treatment. Ebullience certainly radiated through the outer movements, while an elegant second-movement scherzando preceded an exquisite, heart-tugging slow movement. A superbly judged encore came with Reger’s arrangement of one of Bach’s most intimately rhapsodic works for organ, the chorale prelude O Mensch, bewein’.

Barkly Rare Earths has continued its impressive exploration success, hitting significant rare earths mineralisation in 13 of 16 additional holes at its flagship Barkly rare earths project in the Northern Territory. The latest results from its 10,000-metre phase-one drilling campaign have pushed the boundaries of known mineralisation another eight kilometres into previously untested ground. Significant rare earths intercepts have now been recorded in 56 of the 60 holes assayed, spread across a whopping 23km and delivering an impressive strike rate of more than 93 per cent. A reverse circulation drill rig in action at Barkly Rare Earths’ phase-one drilling campaign targeting a massive expansion of its existing 40-million-tonne rare earth resource in the Northern Territory. The drilling program is designed to test for extensions to the project’s existing 40 million-tonne inferred mineral resource grading 2100 parts per million (ppm) total rare earth oxides (TREO). The current inventory is split between the northern and southern deposits, leaving almost 15km of virtually untouched ground in between for the drill bit to explore. That sizeable gap helps explain Barkly’s lofty exploration target of between 200 million and one billion tonnes at a grade of between 1600ppm and 1900ppm TREO. The results served up another swag of eye-catching TREO grades, reinforcing the project’s potential amid accelerating global investment in non-Chinese critical minerals supply chains.

Advertisement

‘This is an intercept rate over 90 per cent across the 60 phase-one holes reported so far, in holes up to 23 kilometres apart.’ Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright The four highest-grade new assays from the latest batch all came from the project’s southern reaches, within and around its existing mineral resource. The standout hole struck a 1.5-metre intercept grading 2171ppm TREO from a shallow 10.5m, including a cracking 0.5-metre section assaying 4550ppm TREO and 1678 magnet rare earth oxides (MREO) from 10.5m. Another notable hit included 2.5m running 1774ppm TREO from 20.5m, which contained a richer slice of 0.5m going a 2599ppm TREO and 845ppm MREO from 21m. Further northwest, five of the first eight holes drilled 8km from previous intercepts also returned significant mineralisation, including the widest phase-one intercept to date of 5.5m at 1035ppm TREO and 343ppm MREO from just 22m downhole. Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright said: “We have now intersected rare earth mineralisation in the northwest, outside the exploration target and six to eight kilometres from previously reported mineralised intercepts. In the south, all eight holes returned significant intercepts... It gives me real confidence in the scale of what we are drilling at Barkly, and we are tendering for a second rig so we can build out the resource faster.”

Advertisement

The company says drilling continues to confirm the deposit’s key characteristics; it appears laterally extensive, with the mineralised horizon now intersected across a massive 23 km. It is shallow and flat-lying, with hits between surface and 38m downhole and is rich in high-value magnet rare earth oxides (MREO), which make up a healthy 29 to 38 per cent of the TREO in the new intercepts. Management says this is consistent with the 34 per cent MREO ratio of the existing inferred mineral resource. MREO’s include neodymium, praseodymium, terbium and dysprosium, some of the most sought-after of the 17 rare earth elements. They are essential for manufacturing high-strength permanent magnets used in electric vehicles and wind turbines. Notably, uranium and thorium levels remain consistently low, between one and three ppm and five to 11 ppm, respectively. Low levels of these radioactive elements are a significant advantage, potentially simplifying processing and reducing costs. The results come as Australia and its allies crank up the race to secure critical minerals supplies and loosen China’s grip on the global rare earths market. The Federal Government recently trumpeted the start of construction at Arafura Rare Earths’ Nolans project, also in the Northern Territory, which has attracted A$1.2 billion in government backing and is tipped to eventually meet up to five per cent of global rare earths demand.

With Australia and the United States committing billions to building alternative supply chains, the geopolitical stars appear to be aligning for explorers such as Barkly. To date, the company has drilled 89 holes for 2168 metres, including 6 re-drills. Samples from a further 26 holes are at or being prepared for the lab, including two re-drills of assayed holes. title: Millions risk fines as key tax deadline nears. Here's what to do
text:
Time is running out for millions of Australians yet to lodge their 2025-26 tax return.

The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) has already received 9 million income tax returns, but it says around 2 million people are yet to submit theirs ahead of the deadline, with late lodgers potentially facing fines.

When is the 2026 tax return deadline?

This year's deadline is Monday 2 November.

The last day of October is traditionally the due date for self-prepared tax returns, but when the 31st falls on a Saturday, the deadline moves to the next business day.

If you are using a tax agent to file your return, the ATO says you must be on their books by 31 October.

ATO assistant commissioner Anita Challen warns taxpayers using this option should also ensure their tax profession is registered with the Tax Practitioners Board.

"Taxpayers should be sceptical of anyone making promises that sound too good to be true," she said.

"No reputable tax professional will encourage you to inflate your deductions, guarantee a refund amount, or claim they can fast-track ATO processing."

What happens if you lodge your tax return late?

If you fail to lodge your return before the due date, the ATO will first try to warn you over the phone or in writing before issuing a penalty.

For taxpayers struggling to file on time or experiencing extenuating circumstances, the ATO says to call and talk to an ATO officer who may be able to offer additional support, including extra time to lodge or pay.

If you are given a fine, you'll receive a notice in writing with the amount and the due date for payment. The payment will be due at least 14 days after the notice is given.

How much is the ATO late lodgement fine?

The fine is calculated based on one penalty unit for every 28 days (or part of that period) that the document is overdue. The maximum for an individual is five penalty units.

A penalty unit for a federal organisation like the ATO is currently valued at $364. So, an individual may be fined up to $1,820.

The range is multiplied for medium and larger entities.

title: Australia's growing cities face an unexpected challenge beneath the surface
text:
In brief Some metropolitan cemeteries are expected to run out of burial space by the early 2030s.

Cremation and alternative forms of deathcare are becoming increasingly common in Australia.

Australians are familiar with the housing crisis, but there's a lesser-known land battle occurring right beneath our feet.

Some metropolitan cemeteries are running out of space, and it's raising questions about the accessibility of burial practices and rise of alternative forms of deathcare.

Among them is Rookwood Cemetery in Sydney's west, which is the largest necropolis in the southern hemisphere.

It rivals the size of many suburbs, spanning more than 280 hectares, and has been operating for almost 160 years.

Rob Smart is the acting CEO of Metropolitan Memorial Parks, which manages eight Crown land cemeteries in NSW, including Rookwood.

He said the company maximises operating space and is trying to acquire more land but almost all of their cemeteries are expected to reach capacity by the early 2030s.

"As our larger sites do run out of land, that puts pressure on all of the other sites that might still have land," he told SBS News.

It's not just Metropolitan Memorial Parks, with many cemeteries in major cities predicting they will reach capacity within the decade.

That's in part due to the growth of urban areas, according to Ben Kelly, the CEO of the Australasian Cemeteries and Crematoria Association.

While cities have continued to grow, Ben Kelly said we haven't been building new cemeteries. Source: Supplied

"You look at Rookwood in Sydney, that was right on the outskirts, and now, that's almost an inner suburb," he said.

"It's just our cities have grown, we just haven't continued building cemeteries."

Another challenge, Kelly said, is that some residents don't want to live next them, while governments had other funding priorities.

"They're worried, they'll ... reduce house prices, that type of thing or they just find them spooky and they're not," he said.

The NSW government is considering converting Carnarvon Golf Club in the Sydney suburb of Lidcombe into a new cemetery, a proposal criticised by some community members, including Auburn MP Lynda Voltz.

READ MORE Kath hosted her late partner Nigel's wake while he was still alive

She addressed NSW parliament in May regarding risks of flooding in the area.

"At first glance, this proposal may be presented as a practical response to the growing demand for burial space but when you take a closer look, a different picture emerges," she said.

"The planning falls short, key risks are being brushed over and yet the environmental consequences are hard to ignore ... flooding here is frequent."

The proposal remains under review.

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, last year there were more than 188,000 registered deaths in the nation. Kelly says roughly 75 to 85 per cent of Australians are now cremated.

But some faith groups, including Islam and Judaism, do not permit the practice.

In 2023, the Vatican updated its guidance on cremation, allowing Catholics to request that a small portion of their relative's ashes be preserved in a "place of significance to them".

Smart believes all Australians should be given the option of a traditional burial.

"Australia is a multicultural country and while we do have a broad range of faiths and cultures within Australia, I think, we need to be able to provide choice," he said.

"To say to people, you can't follow your cultural, your faith-based requirements is very restrictive on the individuals, or the families or the communities."

DIY commemorations

While some cemeteries are running out of space for new burials, Hannah Gould, from the University of Melbourne's DeathTech Research Team, said there is often room to keep cremated remains.

She said the way Australians are approaching death and memorial celebrations is also gradually changing, such as with the rise of 'do it yourself' commemorations.

Hannah Gould says Australians are approaching death commemorations differently than in the past. Source: Supplied

"When it comes to the handling of the body, the vast majority of those processes need to be done by professionals," she said.

"It's not legal in this country to bury somebody or to cremate somebody yourself but kind of everything else now is is increasingly being done by family members and friends.

"You just organise to like get together at the pub with friends, as opposed to having a formal funeral ceremony that's run by a funeral director."

After cremation, ashes can be kept in a permanent place like a cemetery or scattered on private property or certain public areas with permission.

Ashes can also grow into a living memorial tree, be preserved in a memory rock, turned into jewellery, a diamond or even fireworks.

Alternative forms of disposition including sea burials, green or biodegradable burials and full-body human cryonics have taken place around the world.

Upright burials, where the deceased are buried standing, feet first, are also becoming more popular.

Another space-saving measure is renewable tenure, where burial plots are leased for set amounts of time — usually 25, 50 or 99 years — rather than in perpetuity.

If the grave is not renewed after a grace period, the plot can eventually be reused.

It's widely practised in South Australia, while in Western Australia, graves are sold with a 25-year lease known as a grant of right of burial.

Whether a person wants to be cremated or buried, Kelly believes it's important people have conversations about death and disposition while they're still living.

"Trying to plan after the fact of a loved one dying is so difficult," he said.

"So, if they can get in early and have that conversation, you know, put a note on the fridge, a post-it of 'I want to be cremated', it starts a conversation and gets people talking."

title: This tax hasn't changed in 26 years. Some say Australia can no longer afford that
text:
In brief Increasing the GST from 10 to 15 per cent would raise about $76 billion a year, according to the Grattan Institute.

Another recent study found that a GST increase might hurt lower-income households less than commonly thought.

The last time an Australian government owed this much debt, the country was still paying off a world war — except for the COVID-19 pandemic.

As government debt climbs, the Grattan Institute has proposed a controversial solution: hike one tax, cut another, and put more money in welfare recipients' pockets.

In a new report, the think tank argues that raising the country's Goods and Services Tax (GST) and using the money to cut income taxes and boost welfare payments is a solution to the debt issue.

GST is a flat 10 per cent tax applied to the price of most goods and services sold or consumed in Australia.

According to the report, titled Budget reboot: How to fund Australia's future, cost-of-living pressures, growing demand for social services, and higher borrowing costs are the drivers of the Australian government's mounting debt.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

It suggests the situation could worsen in the coming years, with factors such as an ageing population, climate change, and high interest rates forcing the government to spend more.

According to the report, raising GST from 10 per cent to 15 per cent and expanding it to include all food would create a more resilient budget.

Why raising GST has become a 'political no-go zone'

Since its introduction by former prime minister John Howard, which came into effect in July 2000, GST has never increased.

"There are no easy paths back to budget sustainability," Aruna Sathanapally, CEO of Grattan Institute and the report's lead author, said.

"But with smarter spending decisions and a tax system that raises sufficient revenue to care for our ageing population, both current and future generations can be better off.

"Reform on this game-changing scale is challenging, but the prize is worth it: a more secure future for Australia's finances, and for all Australians."

A similar 5 per cent increase plan drafted by economist Richard Holden was pitched by Independent MP Kate Chaney in August 2025.

At the time, Holden told SBS News that compared to other "advanced economies", Australia gets about "twice as much of our revenue from income taxes and about half as much of our income from the GST".

At the time, the Greens labelled the plan "lazy", while the Opposition called it "increasingly brave". Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Labor had not considered a possible GST increase.

"Boosting the GST has become a political no-go zone, in part due to disagreements about how to divvy up the revenue, and concerns it would increase the cost of living," the Grattan Institute report stated.

Where should the revenue go?

The GST increase and expansion will raise about $76 billion a year, according to the Grattan Institute.

The think tank suggests using $58 billion to cut income taxes for low- and middle-income earners and boost welfare payments, which could orchestrate the largest personal income tax cuts in nearly 20 years.

"JobSeeker and Youth Allowance should be raised by 20 per cent, Commonwealth Rent Assistance by 50 per cent, the Parenting Payment by 20 per cent, and pensions by about 8 per cent," the report said.

It suggests allocating the remaining revenue to state governments to shore up their budgets and cut inefficient taxes, such as stamp duty.

It predicts that with the GST increase, most households would pay slightly more in taxes, with larger increases for wealthier and older households.

On the other hand, in estimates, a low-income, single-parent family who rents would be about $150 a week better off, while a higher-income working family would pay $162 a week more in tax.

Would an increase in GST be unfair?

For years, the argument against raising GST was that it would be unfair, particularly to lower-income households.

GST is often described as regressive, in that it takes up a larger share of these households' income than that of higher-income households' income.

This is because higher-income households tend to save more of their income while lower-income households generally spend more of what they earn.

In a July 2025 report, the Australian Council of Social Service argued that increasing the GST to fund income tax cuts "would shift resources from those with the least to those with the most".

However, a recent study by e61–UNSW Policy Research Partnership found that GST may be less regressive than commonly thought. It found households that spend more and those that spend less pay roughly the same share of their spending in GST — about 7.3 per cent.

Examining a household's spending in a year doesn't provide the full picture, the UNSW research partnership says.

Instead, it examined the spending of households across a longer time, taking into account changes in people's circumstances, such as studying, taking parental leave or moving between jobs.

Averaging the years, the gap in GST spending between lower-income and higher-income households narrows.

In other words, the perceived fairness of the GST depends not only on how much people earn, but also on how their spending, saving and longer-term financial position are measured, UNSW says.

The research argues that a reform that includes an increase in GST and paying back the revenue to people "through an unconditional income payment" would be "progressive, irrespective of the measure of household resources".

title: Toxic haze in Southeast Asia worsens amid race to rescue orangutans
text:
In brief Conservation groups are racing to save orangutans in Borneo amid one of Indonesia's worst wildfires.

Pollution levels have risen again and neighbouring countries are badly affected.

Dozens of critically endangered orangutans have been rescued from rampant wildfires burning across Indonesia, as the Borneo residents sue the Indonesian government over negligence in handling the crisis.

The fires have triggered a months-long pollution spell that has closed schools, fuelled a surge in respiratory conditions both among humans and animals, and restricted outdoor activities in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and East Timor.

Pollution levels again ranged from unhealthy to very unhealthy across the region on Sunday, cloaking many areas across southern Southeast Asia in toxic haze.

In Indonesia, groups are working to save wildlife from the fires, including orangutans.

On Saturday, the West Kalimantan conservation agency and Indonesian non-profit YIARI said a team evacuated 51 orangutans from locations in the province from 6 August to 19 October.

Figures from Indonesia's forestry ministry suggested this week that the number rescued over recent months in Kalimantan could be as high as 96.

The latest rescue came on Saturday, when three conservation agencies rescued a 20-year-old male orangutan in Indonesia’s island of Borneo.

"The evacuation process was carried out with great caution," the agencies said.

"After the orangutan was sedated, the medical team immediately conducted a health examination before taking the animal to the ... rehabilitation centre," it said.

Indonesia's transport ministry also said around 2,400 flights across the country have been affected by the haze since mid-August.

"Haze reduces visibility around airports, which can lead to delays, disruptions, and even flight cancellations. Every operational decision is made with safety as the top priority," the ministry said.

A group of Indonesians sue the government

Meanwhile, a group of residents on Borneo have sued the government of negligence in handling forest fires that have been raging there for more than three months.

The hearings in the case started this week, the group’s lawyer said on Friday.

It accuses 27 individuals and agencies, including the Indonesian president and vice president, the ministries of forestry and environment, and law enforcement officials and local authorities.

Both President Prabowo Subianto and Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka have visited areas near the wildfires on Borneo.

Indonesia’s longstanding forest and land fires have worsened this year amid an intensifying El Niño and a prolonged dry season, not only in the Indonesian part of Borneo but also in some regions of Sumatra.

Earlier this week, forest and land fires in Indonesia's Bangka Belitung province in Sumatra spread into a densely populated residential area, damaging at least 300 houses and forcing the evacuation of 500 people.

'Unhealthy' air quality in Singapore

The fire scorched vast expanses of land and has polluted the air as far away as Malaysia and Singapore.

Pollution levels have ranged from unhealthy to very unhealthy across the region on Sunday, cloaking many areas across southern Southeast Asia in toxic haze.

Swiss-based air quality monitor IQAir again ranked Singapore and Kuala Lumpur among the world's five most polluted major cities.

Months of sustained wildfires in Indonesia have blanketed Southeast Asian countries in hazardous haze, with Singapore and Malaysia badly hit. Source: AAP / Then Chih Wey

From 8 am to 9 am local time, the air quality index reached 202, rated "very unhealthy" in Singapore. By noon, it had improved to 163, still in the "unhealthy" range.

At AA Alive, a medical equipment company based just outside of Kuala Lumpur, employees are working at full capacity to deliver oxygen bottles, with officials saying sales were rocketing.

"We have seen a 35 per cent increase in sales because of the haze," Rafina Firdaus, a member of AA Alive's sales team, told AFP during a visit.

"When I started in the industry, I was shocked to see so many patients who need oxygen tanks," she said.

The company supplies patients with both oxygen tanks and oxygen concentrators. An oxygen tank can run for about three hours of continuous use, while a concentrator can be used for about 24 hours.

Md Noor Bin Bujang spent more than a month in hospital and received his first oxygen concentrator on Thursday evening.

He told AFP that without the oxygen-providing equipment he would have "a shortness of breath, especially with the haze".

title: Why is the haze so bad in Southeast Asia this year?
text:
Months of sustained wildfires in Indonesia have caused a spike in respiratory illnesses and blanketed several Southeast Asian countries in hazardous haze, with Singapore and Malaysia also hit badly over the last week.

The pollution has stoked political tensions across the region, with officials questioning Jakarta's handling of the fires as well as its reluctance to accept help from its neighbours.

What is the source of the haze?

The haze is made up of fumes from forest and peatland fires across Indonesia, most notably on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra, which are made up of dense forests and vast stretches of peatland that are especially prone to fire during the dry season, which usually runs from April to October.

The region is also currently under the influence of severe "super-El Niño" weather conditions, which brought additional heat and dryness and caused wildfires to spread more quickly.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The last time Indonesia experienced such intense fires was 2015, when El Niño conditions were similarly severe.

How much damage have the fires done?

Official data on the extent of the land damaged by fire has not been updated since July, when 202,000 hectares had been burned.

But according to environment group Auriga, more than 637,000 hectares were damaged from January to August this year, nine times the area of Singapore.

Deforestation monitor Nusantara Atlas put the figure even higher at nearly 900,000 hectares.

How bad is the haze?

Emissions from Indonesia's fires have been the highest in the world for a month, making up almost half the global total over the last seven days, according to data from Fire Emissions Watch, a portal developed by the European Union's Copernicus climate monitoring service.

Indonesia's air pollution index has shown some areas of Borneo and Sumatra registering pollution levels of over 1,000, with readings of 300 or more already categorised as hazardous.

Singapore's 1-hour PM2.5 reading hit a high of 284 micrograms per cubic metre in the western part of the island state last week, entering the National Environmental Agency's "very high" band for the first time this year.

The number of cases of respiratory illness linked to the fires surged to 283,270 in seven Indonesian provinces alone as of 13 October, more than double the 113,336 reported as of 9 September, the country's health ministry data showed.

Many schools in Indonesia, neighbouring Timor-Leste and some states in Malaysia were forced to close, and nearly 2,000 flights in Indonesia have been affected between 11 August and 12 October.

What is Indonesia doing to tackle the fires?

The Indonesian government says it is doing everything it can.

Over 60,000 personnel have been deployed to fight the fires, and around 50 aircraft have engaged in water bombing and cloud seeding operations.

The government plans to employ more forest rangers to prevent fires, and has vowed to restore its peatland ecosystem, where fires can smoulder underground for much longer and at lower temperatures.

It says it has cracked down on law-breaking enterprises and restricted the use of fire to clear farmland. Police officials have said 223 individuals and nine companies could face action for their involvement in starting forest fires.

Why is Indonesia being criticised?

The Indonesian government has come under increasing international pressure to do more to tackle fires, both before and after they start.

Its crackdown on the use of fire to clear land has not completely eliminated the practice. Rapid deforestation to make way for growing crops, most notably to increase palm oil production, has also raised the risk of fires by draining underground water sources and drying out the soil.

READ MORE Thousands of hectares burnt as El Niño intensifies Indonesia's dry season

The government's reluctance to declare the situation a national disaster, which would allow it to deploy resources more quickly, has also been questioned. It has also not yet accepted offers of help from both Malaysia and Singapore.

How long will the fires and haze last?

Indonesian authorities say that, despite their best efforts, the situation will only be contained when there is sustained rainfall in the region.

The dry season started earlier this year and has lasted longer than usual. Rain usually starts in October, but forecasts say it will be delayed until November.

The effects of El Niño are expected to last until the first quarter of 2027, but the upcoming rain season will help diminish the impact of the fires, Indonesia's weather agency said.

title: Major Woodside gas project paused after Greenpeace protest off Western Australia
text:
The operations at Australian oil and gas giant, Woodside's $12.5 billion Scarborough project in Western Australia have stopped after Greenpeace staged a protest at a floating platform.

"That opportunity was there with a new leader, but these events and internal disagreements have taken their toll. It's been a very tough start to Senator Shoebridge's leadership."

'A real test'

The latest challenge came on Wednesday, when WA Greens senator Jordon Steele-John took leave from the party as allegations related to his comments about women triggered an inquiry.

While Steele-John "utterly" rejected the characterisation, which he said tried to "assert" him as someone he wasn't, the Sydney Morning Herald reported that the WA Greens branch had allegedly maintained a crisis communications dossier, instructing staff how to comment on any allegations made about Steele-John's conduct around women, for a decade.

WA Greens has said in a statement that it considers "any allegations of this nature to be serious and concerning" and that the "matter needs to be resolved via a fair, timely and independent investigation".

Ghazarian said the allegations "have the potential to destabilise the party and have a significant negative impact".

"This is going to be a real test," he told SBS News.

"Senator Shoebridge came into the leadership with a reputation as an effective communicator and parliamentary performer. He will need to draw on all of those skills.

"Ultimately, this is going to be a real test of his leadership."

Shoebridge has refused to say whether the party will publish the findings of the inquiry into allegations against Steele-John.

He also said he was unaware of past complaints about the senator until a letter from seven Greens members landed on his desk this week.

A 'destabilising' debate

The controversy around Steele-John came just days after the party reportedly faced internal disagreement over its policy on military aid to Ukraine.

In an interview with the Sydney Morning Herald during his first week as leader, Shoebridge said, "we don’t support military aid to Ukraine", while the party also "oppose Russia’s illegal invasion".

The stance drew criticism not only from other politicians and the Ukrainian community, but also from a high-profile party member.

Sarah Hanson-Young, the party's Senate business manager, who lost the leadership contest to Shoebridge, told ABC's 7.30, "We need to be doing everything we can to support the people in Ukraine."

When pressed on whether that includes providing military equipment, she responded, "If that's the support that people need in order to defend themselves from the invasion of Russia, I think Australians need to support that."

About 70 per cent of Australians support providing military aid to Ukraine, according to a poll by the Lowy Institute.

Ghazarian said the "debate about Ukraine has been destabilising for the Greens".

"They need to explain their policy positions clearly and be on the front foot when it comes to discussing public policy.

"Instead, they seem to have been on the back foot ... It is a very testing period for the Greens and for the new leader."

'Deep' internal divisions

The challenges for Shoebridge started almost as soon as the 11-member party committee chose him as its leader, after winning the party's first contested leadership ballot.

He beat former deputy leader Mehreen Faruqi seven votes to four, and Hanson-Young was knocked out in the first round.

In response, Faruqi said she was "disappointed the party room chose another direction" and that "many others will feel the same way", signalling possible divisions in the party.

In a video on social media, Hanson-Young also said, "God, politics can be brutal".

"The Greens have always had two broad strands within the party," Ghazarian said.

"One has been more focused on pragmatism and working with other political parties within parliament to achieve policy outcomes. The other has been more activist in its approach, with a stronger focus on changing grassroots behaviours and actions.

"Like other political parties, the Greens have internal divisions, and they can potentially be quite deep."

At the federal election, the party lost ground and has struggled to regain momentum, losing three of its four lower house seats — including the Melbourne seat held by its then-leader, Adam Bandt.

Now the Greens seem to have been overshadowed in the public debate by the attention focused on One Nation.

Ghazarian said the upcoming Victorian state elections in November "will be a significant test for the Greens brand".

"This is occurring at a time when the Victorian Labor Party appears to be losing support, the Coalition appears to be gaining support, and One Nation is also polling strongly," he said.

"This election will be a real test.

"Any faltering by the Greens could prove costly because it is always difficult to win seats back once they are lost."

title: The Bali venues taking a stand against bad tourist behaviour
text:
IN BRIEF Locals are reporting a rise in bad behaviour by tourists on Bali.

Bali was Australia's top holiday destination last year, with over 1.6 million people travelling to the island.

Shirtless diners, feet on chairs, arrogant tones and speeding motorbikes — a growing number of restaurants have "really had enough" of these bad tourist behaviours in Bali and are now taking action.

It's gotten so bad that Herzza Rahmadhani Duha, the owner of popular restaurant OUFFF in Canggu on Bali's south coast, told SBS Indonesian she's had to put a set of rules on the venue's door.

"If they don't follow the rules, they will be asked to leave immediately."

OUFF is one of several venues in Bali that have announced their expectations of guests on social media, coming together to make a statement.

It comes as locals report a rise in bad tourist behaviour on the island.

"They exploit that hospitality and do not repay it with kindness and respect."

'You are not welcome here'

Bali was Australia's top holiday destination last year, attracting more than 1.6 million travellers, according to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade.

In September, an Australian tourist was deported after allegedly being caught on CCTV engaging in a sexual act in a residential driveway.

Rahmadhani Duha said she believes there is "one main reason" for bad tourism behaviour in Indonesia.

"Indonesians are very kind, perhaps even too friendly. People like this would probably not behave the same way in Europe or Western Europe. But here, they feel they can do whatever they want because Indonesians are too accommodating," she said.

"If you ride dangerously in our neighbourhood, or your motorcycle has a modified or loud exhaust, you are not welcome here," DELLA TERRA, a restaurant at Pererenan, just north of Canggu, has posted on Instagram.

Restaurants against dangerous driving

Motorcycle and scooter accidents are very common in Bali, where many tourists prefer to rent a motorcycle. In 2024, the Bali Regional Police reported 142 traffic accidents that involved foreigners.

In recent years, local authorities have announced plans to restrict motorcycle access for tourists,

Openhouse cafe in Pererenan has partnered directly with the village council to fight against dangerous driving in the area.

"If you feel the need to speed around the roads in the local community, you can go somewhere else; in fact, just leave the island," the post says.

title: 'It was an honour': Katie Zacharia breaks silence after White House sacking
text:
In brief Katie Zacharia has been dropped as White House press secretary after less than a week in the job.

On top of a poor first briefing and questions over her legal credentials, she also mocked China.

Katie Zacharia has said she wished more Americans appreciated United States President Donald Trump, in her first public statement since she was forced out of her White House secretary role after less than a week in the job.

In a statement posted on X, Zacharia said it was an "honour" to work with Trump, who she described as a "kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man".

"I wish more Americans appreciated him," she wrote.

"No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to."

Zacharia was "let go" and was "transitioning out" of the press secretary position, according to reports from two separate White House officials.

It was a brutal close to her tumultuous five-day stint in the high-profile role, which included a series of public blunders that added to distractions for Trump.

She faced days of questions ‌about her legal credentials and criticism of her performance in a news briefing and interviews.

"Can confirm", a White House official told the Agence France-Presse news agency, after Fox News reported that Zacharia, 41, was "transitioning out".

The writing was on the wall earlier when Trump made clear he was ready to see his newly minted spokesperson go.

"I said, 'Katie, is this for you?'" Trump told reporters. "I said, 'Katie, you don't have to do this'... I said to her, 'Honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider.'"

Zacharia only began her job five days ago, taking over from the combative Karoline Leavitt, who helped Trump reshape White House coverage by bringing in more friendly outlets and fiercely attacking critical media.

Zacharia had got off to a rocky start with her debut press room briefing Tuesday morning.

It lasted less than 15 minutes, beginning with a remarkably slow reading out of what she said were Trump's many accomplishments — then taking just three questions from journalists.

She then was plunged into controversy when it emerged that her previous claims to be a lawyer were not true.

The kerfuffle is a distraction for 80-year-old Trump as he flies around the country trying to boost Republican candidates ahead of the 3 November congressional midterm elections, with polls predicting a drubbing.

The Republican leader himself also faces ever-lower polls as Americans sour over the war against Iran, inflation and perceptions of corruption.

Controversy over Zacharia's legal credentials

Zacharia had described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and on social media, and listed herself as general counsel of a California-based conservative nonprofit.

While she does have a law degree from a California university, she acknowledged on Thursday she had failed the bar exam, a prerequisite for practising law in the US.

She embarked on a series of damage-control interviews on Trump-friendly outlets, but they did no good.

In one of them, Fox News' Sean Hannity, a close Trump ally, appeared dismissive of Zacharia.

He asked the press secretary if she ever retook the bar exam. She replied, "I did not."

"It was never my intent to go into the practice of law," she said.

In another interview Thursday with pro-Trump outlet Real America's Voice, Zacharia said she had registered to take the bar exam but was "distracted and overwhelmed" by plans to move to China with her husband.

Zacharia said "many people in the field" had assured her that she could "label myself a lawyer," given her law degree.

Press secretary's potty-mouthed remarks

"Fox and Friends", which often conducts friendly interviews with Trump administration officials, was unusually direct on Saturday when a host asked Zacharia if she still had the confidence of the president.

"I hope to be able to build the trust and confidence of everyone around me," she said, sidestepping the question.

Zacharia further stirred controversy on Thursday when she disparaged China, whose leader Xi Jinping was recently Trump's guest in a pomp-filled Washington visit.

The press secretary recalled the perception in 2016 was that China would soon overtake the US.

"I remember this very distinctly, having just come from China, thinking: 'How is China the next country on the horizon? They don't even have proper toilets,'" she told right-wing influencer Jack Posobiec in an interview.

Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning responded Friday that Zacharia should "visit China more often".

Australia’s largest listed data centre developer has warned investors that power supply delays, likely caused by community opposition, will hit the development of its flagship West Footscray facility. Data centre giant NextDC sought a trading halt in its ASX-listed shares on Monday telling investors it needed to assess the impact of the delay in getting power to its M3 data centre in West Footscray. NextDC’s M3 data centre in West Footscray, Melbourne, in March this year. Joe Armao The company did not give a reason for the delay but analysts tipped it was likely the result of a fierce community blockade in Melbourne’s inner-west last month that brought a multi-million-dollar power pole expansion by electricity distributor Jemena to a standstill. Citigroup analyst Siraj Ahmed said in a briefing to investors that the trading halt likely related to electricity distributor Jemena’s pause on that project.

NextDC’s market admission is the clearest evidence yet that Victoria’s rapid push to attract power-hungry artificial intelligence infrastructure has run directly into grid constraints and suburban resistance. The M3 facility in West Footscray is designed to eventually span 10 hectares across an industrial pocket directly adjacent to residential homes. The data centre already takes up five hectares and is undergoing a $750 million expansion. But feeding the site required network operator Jemena to replace standard wooden electricity poles with 15-metre-high concrete structures carrying 66,000 volts down residential streets in West Footscray and neighbouring Yarraville.

Neither Jemena nor NextDC has confirmed the rollout was directly linked to the power pole pause. That rollout ground to a halt in Yarraville last month following direct action by local residents, who blockaded contractor trucks with parked cars, ignored door-knocks, and filled excavation pits to stop the high-voltage lines reaching the NextDC site. Then-premier Jacinta Allan with NextDC chief executive Craig Scroggie in 2025 in one of the data centre’s Melbourne premises. Justin McManus Jemena bowed to the pressure and has since paused work in Yarraville to allow for consultation, leaving the high-capacity power route unfinished. Many of the West Footscray power poles designed to carry the far higher voltage had already been installed. In its letter to the ASX, signed by NextDC company secretary Michael Helmer, the company said its board had not yet met to consider the full implications of the power delay. The trading halt will remain in place until Wednesday or until a full announcement is made.

Accelerate Resources has unearthed high-grade manganese rock chips grading as much as 59.6 per cent and identified a completely new discovery at its Woodie Woodie North project in Western Australia’s prolific East Pilbara region. The results from the Faris and the freshly-minted Sea Turtle prospects have lit up a 12-kilometre-long mineralised corridor that has astonishingly only ever been tested by very shallow holes drilled 30 years ago. The discovery comes at a time when both government and industry are paying closer attention to securing manganese supply chains. Outcropping high-grade manganese at Accelerate Resources’ Woodie Woodie North project, just 55km north of Consolidated Minerals’ long-running Woodie Woodie manganese mine in the Pilbara. Surface sampling at the Faris prospect bagged a suite of impressive assays, with four rock chips grading between a hefty 53.9 per cent and a cracking 59.6 per cent manganese. Importantly, the samples were also low in impurities, with iron levels between just 0.7 and one per cent. Notably, the high-grade outcrop at Faris, just two kilometres south-east of the company’s Area 42 deposit, sits directly above shallow, historic drilling that delivered high-grade hits of 11m running 28.4 per cent manganese from just one-metre downhole and 3m assaying 39.1 per cent manganese from surface.

‘Together, they support a rapidly emerging high grade manganese trend over 12km between our Area 42 deposit and Gingarrigan and El Largo.’ Accelerate Resources chief executive officer Luke Meter Adding to the tally, the field geos also clocked a new discovery at the company’s Sea Turtle prospect. Mapping has defined a large iron and manganese alteration system measuring 650m by 400m that has previously never been drill tested. Rock chips from two new outcrops returned grades up to 31.4 per cent manganese, confirming the system is fertile. Accelerate Resources chief executive officer Luke Meter said: “The ongoing discovery of high-grade manganese along this exciting 12km trend continues to support the continuity of mineralisation through this extensive belt. The more we map new targets on the ground, the more we find. Faris has delivered rock chips all above 53 per cent manganese with very low iron, sitting directly over high-grade historic drilling. At Sea Turtle, our geology team has found two new manganese outcrops inside a large alteration system that has not previously been drilled.” The new discoveries form part of a systematic exploration push and follow the company’s savvy move last month to consolidate 100 per cent ownership of the Woodie Woodie North project, clearing the decks of all legacy payments and royalties. The scrip-based deal means the company can now capture all the upside from these and any other new discoveries. Management says the simplified structure will also better support any potential funding, offtake or partnering discussions down the track. The Woodie Woodie North project sits 55km north of Consolidated Minerals’ long-running Woodie Woodie manganese mine and already hosts a maiden inferred mineral resource of 1.2 million tonnes grading 19.1 per cent manganese. That resource lies alongside a hefty exploration target of between 5.3 and 10.7 million tonnes (Mt) at grades of 10 to 19 per cent manganese.

Being on the doorstep of a major, multi-decade mining operation is an enviable position for any explorer. Perhaps more tantalising, geology pays little attention to tenement boundaries, with the company believing it may be sitting on a significant extension of the same mineralised system that has made its neighbour a globally significant producer. Accelerate is also actively de-risking the development pathway for its cornerstone Area 42 deposit, which holds a resource of 0.7Mt at 20.7 per cent manganese. Recent large-diameter drilling for metallurgical testwork hit thick zones of visual mineralisation, including a 72-metre downhole span in one hole from just 5.6m below surface. Canberra recently moved to bolster Australia’s critical-minerals policy by establishing a Critical Minerals Strategic Reserve, drawing on a $5 billion funding facility to support domestic supply chains. With manganese a key component in both steel and the growing battery market, the commodity is attracting significant strategic interest. Accelerate’s focus on manganese is part of a dual-pronged strategy, which also includes the Balagundi gold project near Kalgoorlie. In a nod to its two key commodities, the company plans to rebrand as Mango Metals, a combination of manganese and gold. Next steps in the Pilbara include a 3000-metre discovery drilling program at its nearby Gingarrigan manganese prospect, expected to kick off in the coming days. The Minns government will intervene to give a Hunter Valley coal mine a licence to dig up millions of tonnes more each year despite a seismic High Court ruling that found its approval was invalid because it had failed to reckon with emissions from Australian coal burnt overseas. Premier Chris Minns announced on Monday that the NSW government would step in to give MACH Energy legislated approval to increase production at the Mount Pleasant coal mine to 16.5 million tonnes a year, from its current limit of 12.5 million tonnes, until 2032. The Minns government has intervened to give MACH Energy’s Mount Pleasant Coal Mine Operations near Muswellbrook an expanded approval. Kate Geraghty Minns said the decision came after MACH Energy told the government it was preparing to sack half its workforce – about 400 people – before Christmas if its approval was not expanded. In return for boosting the mine’s annual production limit, the government said the company had agreed to sign a jobs guarantee that would establish a legal obligation to maintain staffing levels. The intervention comes after the High Court ruled a fortnight ago that a 2022 approval by the NSW Independent Planning Commission was invalid because it had failed to properly consider the climate impact of coal exported overseas from the mine.

Advertisement

The ruling – which found the IPC had not properly considered the impact of so-called “scope 3 emissions” – led to immediate calls from the Coalition and One Nation for Labor to urgently pass new laws overruling the High Court. Related Article Updated

High Court of Australia ‘Pandora’s box’: High Court decision could reopen coal mine approval cases Despite initially playing down the need for legal change, Minns said Indonesian billionaire Anthoni Salim’s MACH Energy informed the government it was preparing to sack the workers before Christmas. That was because it had scaled up its workforce to prepare for the increase in its production limit to 21 million tonnes a year as approved by the IPC. “These are not easy decisions,” Minns said. “They’re incredibly difficult, and I’ve agonised over this one. “The truth of the matter is there’s some people who say that the only thing to worry about is industry and jobs in all and every circumstance, and there are others who say you should only be worrying about the environment in any and all circumstances … we have to do both.

Advertisement

“We have to approach these things in a commonsense way and draw conclusions so that we’re making progress towards our climate goals, while at the same time not tipping hundreds and hundreds of families onto the scrap heap weeks before Christmas.” NSW Natural Resources Minister Courtney Houssos said the new legislation – which will be introduced during the next sitting fortnight – would include requirements to limit scope 3 emissions in line with the IPC’s recent Hunter Valley Operations mine approval. It means that, in effect, the company can only export coal to countries that are signatories to the Paris climate agreement. The decision prompted immediate backlash from environmental groups, which accused the government of interfering with independent planning rules. Greens MP Sue Higginson said Labor had capitulated to “threats and taken the side of the billionaire coal company over the community”. “This is an incredible new low for the Minns Labor government, bypassing the planning process and the law as laid down by the High Court of Australia,” she said. “One thing is clear, under Labor the coal mining giants are writing the laws, and they are laws that will cause significant unassessed climate pollution and hurt communities.”

Advertisement

Lock the Gate national co-ordinator Georgina Woods called it “cynical and dangerous political interference in the planning system”, accusing Labor of “manufacturing a crisis to give special treatment to a coal company”. Related Article Climate policy ‘Triply nervous’: Massive coal mine braced for challenge after High Court ruling “There is no threat to jobs at Mount Pleasant, which already has approval to stay open for another six years,” she said. Labor is facing significant pressure from One Nation in the Hunter Valley. Asked if his government would have made the same decision if an election was not looming, Minns said: “I believe we would have. “What I would say in relation to that very fair question is: Look at the government’s record over the last six months,” he said, referring to a series of manufacturing announcements in the Hunter valley and the Tomago Aluminium bailout.

“We’re a Labor government. We do need to protect jobs.” Minns denied the government was undermining rules around the independent assessment of mines, saying the impact of the High Court judgment on MACH Energy’s expansion would still need to be worked out in the lower courts. He called it a “partial approval to keep pace with the current workforce that’s on the ground in that community”. “It’s a difficult decision to make,” he said. “In normal circumstances, you wouldn’t want to do it. You’d want the court to make the decision before any expansion or a decision from the company. Great Southern Mining has hit paydirt with maiden reverse circulation (RC) drilling at its Amy Clarke prospect within the Duketon gold project near Laverton in Western Australia, intersecting high-grade gold along a previously defined 4.7-kilometre mineralised corridor. The company says the results reinforce the prospect’s potential, sitting just 12km from Regis Resources’ Garden Well processing facility. The 18-hole, 2248-metre campaign tested higher-grade zones identified by earlier aircore drilling. It appears to have done its job, returning a clutch of impressive near-surface intercepts along strike and at depth, extending mineralisation down-dip by up to 50m and broadening areas of higher-grade gold. Reverse circulation drilling at Great Southern Mining’s Amy Clarke prospect within the Duketon Gold Project in Western Australia. The headline result came from a hole that delivered 5m grading 6.71 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 51m, including a richer three-metre core going 10.4g/t gold. Other notable hits likely to make management smile included 2m at 8.92g/t within a broader 11-metre interval grading 1.86g/t gold from 45m. A third returned multiple mineralised zones, the best of which was 8m at 1.44g/t from 67m, featuring 2m at 4.7g/t gold.

Advertisement

‘Amy Clarke is an emerging discovery with immense upside. The gold starts from surface and continues to the extent of the drilling in the fresh rock.’ Great Southern Mining managing director Matthew Keane Further results show the system’s breadth, with intercepts of 5m at 1.81g/t gold from 61m, 2m at 1.41g/t from a very shallow 7m and multiple one-metre slices grading more than 2g/t gold. Reported intervals are downhole lengths, with true widths not yet confirmed. The company says while drilling remains shallow, averaging less than 100m below surface, with mineralisation observed from surface in the oxidised, or weathered, horizon and extending at depth into fresh rock. Geologically, the gold at Amy Clarke is associated with quartz veining and disseminated or coarse pyrite. According to Great Southern, the prospect lies in a high-strain structural corridor, generally near contacts between different rock types, with the structures currently modelled as steeply east-dipping, a classic setting for gold deposition in the Eastern Goldfields. Great Southern managing director Matthew Keane said: “The Company’s aggressive 2026 RC drilling campaign has delivered strong results across three key targets, incorporating Amy Clarke, the Golden Boulder discovery and Mon Ami, with all three returning high-grade intercepts and material extensions to known mineralisation.”

Advertisement

With a successful maiden RC campaign in the bag, detailed geological and structural mapping is underway, alongside multi-element geochemistry of selected intervals, to better understand the controls on mineralisation and home in on the highest-grade zones. Great Southern says it has already started planning for the next phase, likely to include follow-up RC drilling and potential diamond drilling. Initial drilling is expected to focus on open lodes in the northern part of Amy Clarke and the central section of the 4.7-kilometre trend. The system remains open to the south, where little drilling has been undertaken beyond the company’s southernmost holes, leaving a substantial stretch of prospective ground largely untested. The latest results add another string to Great Southern’s bow at Duketon, complementing its nearby Golden Boulder discovery, where historic production averaged an eye-watering grade of 28.6g/t gold and the company has since outlined mineralisation along 3.5km of strike. The junior explorer is awaiting assays from another 6000m of ongoing drilling at the southern end of Golden Boulder and the Golden Boulder East trend, 3km southwest of Amy Clarke. Amy Clarke is interpreted to lie along the same structural trend that hosts Regis’ Erlistoun open pit mine, about 3km to the north, which contains a 320,000-ounce resource grading 1.9g/t gold. The Garden Well processing facility, with a capacity of five million tonnes per annum, is 12km to the northeast. The broader Duketon Greenstone Belt is no stranger to big gold discoveries, with mining heavyweight Regis Resources identifying more than eight million ounces of gold resources across the region. Great Southern’s tenure includes significant sections of the major shear zones that are known to host the majority of the deposits across the belt.

Advertisement

In a gold-rich neighbourhood where proximity to processing infrastructure can be worth its weight in gold, Great Southern is assembling an increasingly enticing collection of prospects on the doorstep of established mining operations. With Amy Clarke shaping up as another potential discovery and a swag of fresh assays from Golden Boulder still to come, the company’s Duketon gold story looks to have plenty more chapters left to write.
