title: Tame Impala’s spectacular show a kaleidoscope of colour and controlled chaos
text:
Advertisement

Key points MUSIC: Tame Impala puts on a colour and laser-filled show at Rod Laver Arena

JAZZ: The Melbourne International Jazz Festival has kicked off for 2026

OPERA: Opera Australia returns to the State Theatre with The Wagner Gala Concert

MUSIC: Mozart, Salieri and Pleyel shows the Australian Brandenburg Orchestra at its best

DANCE: Lucy Guerin returns to the stage with Place Dances

MUSIC

Tame Impala ★★★★

Rod Laver Arena, October 14 Kevin Parker loves a laser. In a 2015 Rolling Stone interview with the Tame Impala doyen, it’s revealed that a bedroom in his Fremantle home – the same house in which he’s then just self-made his brilliant third LP Currents – is filled with dozens of automated stage lights on stands. Parker explains that instead of complaining about a light show he’s not happy with, he decided to teach himself how to design his own. Kevin Parker’s meticulousness is all over the spectacular Tame Impala live experience. Richard Clifford Checks out. Parker’s meticulousness is all over the spectacular Tame Impala live experience. While he presents as the chill savant who’s wandered onto the spaceship stage at the rave, armed with a casual jumper, floppy hair and a selection of monster hits etched into the universal songbook, an enormous rig of tessellated lights and lasers unfolds in increasingly eye-boggling configurations. It all makes the springy house chords of Breathe Deeper, arena-singalong melody of Feels Like I Only Go Backwards, and mirror-maze of groove feints that propel guitar stomper Elephant feel like the apex of the live music experience. A bedroom producer’s fantasy in full flight.

Advertisement

Grittier electronic tracks from new LP Deadbeat are offset by the sweet tenor of Parker’s voice. Dracula and Afterthought – both with nods to Michael Jackson’s Thriller – are fun highlights, Parker stepping off-stage in pop star mode to slap hands with fans. The squealing crowd skews much younger than the 40-year-old Parker, suggesting his arc from airy psych-rock into a signature DIY-brand of mainstream pop has energised new generations of fans. Parker’s spectacular Rod Laver Arena show is a bedroom producer’s fantasy in full flight. Richard Clifford Mid-set, Parker ambles backstage, followed by a cameraman who films him appearing to urinate in a bathroom. He re-emerges by the mixing desk on a lamp-lit stage to sip from a can of Melbourne Bitter and sing insular Deadbeat tracks Ethereal Connection and Not My World, surrounded by 14,000 people waving phone torches. In the shadows, his longtime band chug away in service to a set list that rarely changes and a frontman who lets his lasers do the talking. Where I’m sitting, the sound mix is overwhelmed by shuddering bass frequencies – a disappointment for enjoying the production of a famously meticulous sound nerd. But the annoyance fades as we cascade into mass singalongs Let It Happen, Eventually, and The Less I Know the Better, each exploding with a kaleidoscope of confetti, colour and controlled chaos around this clever Peter Pan from Perth at the centre of it all.

Reviewed by Marcus Teague

Advertisement

JAZZ

Melbourne International Jazz Festival

Opening weekend, October 16-18 The opening weekend of the Melbourne International Jazz Festival was overflowing with premieres, festival commissions and first-time collaborations. Joey Alexander (left) performs alongside Young Monk and Skylar Tang (trumpet). Duncographic In Friday night’s double bill at the Recital Centre (curated in partnership with New York’s Jazz at Lincoln Center), the phenomenal Indonesian pianist Joey Alexander fronted two separate ensembles. The first was an international iteration of Young Monk, a jazz project in which rising stars of the future interpret the music of Thelonious Monk. Here, Alexander and the superb New York-based trumpeter Skylar Tang were joined by three gifted Melbourne players.

Advertisement

Alexander and Tang both spoke earnestly and eloquently about their love of Monk’s music, and their passion radiated from the stage as they played. Local players Toby Barrett, Lily Appelt and Ebs Daramola clearly relished the opportunity to perform with international peers on a festival stage, and the whole ensemble buzzed with energy and vitality. Xani Kolac performs at the festival. Max Roux The second half featured Alexander with his eponymous ensemble, which allowed the pianist to shine in a set of exuberant originals. Yes, the preternatural virtuosity that brought him to the world’s attention when he was still a child was on dazzling display. But the rhapsodic cascades that poured from the 23-year-old’s hands never came across as empty showmanship. On the contrary, each sparkling melodic extension, harmonic exploration or spirited interaction with his bandmates felt like a natural expression of an artist doing what he was born to do, with irrepressible joy and unshakeable conviction. On Saturday, the New York-based Cuban saxophonist Yosvany Terry led another specially assembled outfit alongside his brother, bassist Yunior Terry (now based in Melbourne), US pianist Brett Williams and drummer Julian Miltenberger. Together, they formed a marvellously potent and muscular ensemble – at times urgent and propulsive, at times breezily buoyant. The final tune (Summer Relief) featured Yosvany on shekere, summoning Afro-Cuban deities with intricate rhythms and invocatory chants before inviting the band – and the audience – to join him in this contemporary reinvention of ancient rituals. Later that night, electric violinist and composer Xani Kolac premiered a compelling new suite, Kołacz, at Howler in Brunswick. Kolac is the festival’s Take Note artist for 2026, and used her commission to delve into her Polish heritage and create a deeply personal work exploring her search for identity and belonging.

Advertisement

As she explained from the stage, this search also encompassed her quest for acceptance as an artist whose music refuses to be bound by genre. It eventually became a celebration of her distinctive creative voice. Using violin, accordion (played by Tuulikki Bartosik), bass, drums, vocals and an array of pedals and effects, her quartet conjured a constantly changing sound world incorporating folk-like whimsy, experimental rock, abstract sound art and boisterous East European dance. Sunday brought another premiere: Eugene Ball’s Continuum, commissioned by ABC Jazz to celebrate the 50th anniversary of Jazztrack. Designed to reflect the impact and legacy of this long-running national radio program, Ball’s masterfully written and beautifully realised suite featured an eight-piece ensemble gliding across stately big-band-style tunes, strutting with jaunty classic-jazz vigour, bristling with angular precision and plunging into pools of bold, free-form drama. The Shai Maestro Trip perform at Chapel Off Chapel. Max Roux Then came the Shai Maestro Trio’s sublime performance at Chapel Off Chapel. This was not a premiere or a new collaboration (though singer Gian Slater joined the band as a guest for one exquisite tune, Gloria). It was, however, the most heart-swelling, spirit-lifting encounter you could imagine. The chapel’s illuminated stained-glass windows provided an appropriate backdrop for this music, which had a luminous and often transportive quality. Using intuition as their guide, Maestro and his supremely empathetic bandmates (Reuben Rogers on bass and Ofri Nehemya on drums) built jewel-like melodies into soulfully ecstatic grooves or flamenco-fuelled climaxes as they swelled and surged in restless waves, sweeping the audience into their orbit and holding us utterly spellbound.

Reviewed by Jessica Nicholas

The Melbourne International Jazz Festival continues until Sunday

NOTE: No star rating has been applied to the above review

Advertisement

OPERA

The Wagner Gala Concert ★

Opera Australia, Ian Potter State Theatre, October 16 The State Theatre has only been closed for about 2½ years, but to Melbourne’s opera community, it’s felt like an age. Orchestra Victoria performs Opera Australia’s Wagner Gala on October 16. Jeff Busby The national opera company has been something of a wand’ring minstrel in that time, turning up at The Regent Theatre and Hamer Hall, before making a short-lived sojourn to Margaret Court Arena, where its 2024 production of Tosca went out in straight sets. OA sought to make a triumphant return to the newly named Ian Potter State Theatre with an all-Wagner gala. For something so long in the making, it was frustratingly underdeveloped.

Advertisement

Orchestra Victoria did its diligent best, but it felt as though the players and German conductor Michael Güttler had just met that morning – most musicians barely looked up from their scores at him, and some looked sullen. Güttler made strident gestures at them in return, the resultant interpretations of the many overtures and preludes a torrent of Wagnerian generality. This is music that should stir the soul. It was fine. Editor's pick Live music Baker Boy showered with gifts by young fans at milestone gig English soprano Catherine Foster was merely going through the motions, Russian tenor Sergey Skorokhodov was clearly unwell and coughing so frequently it appeared doubtful he would make it through his final aria. Australian baritone James Clayton had the least to do but was the most commendable. This program felt a million miles away from a party. We were meant to be celebrating opera being back in this beautiful theatre, so why was this whole affair so sombre? This gala was not opera for the people. The absence of surtitles made an already forbidding program needlessly inaccessible. Most of the audience were left to decipher some big German feelings, delivered by a mostly international cast, and wonder what it’s all got to do with the city of Melbourne and the reopening of our beloved theatre. This program did not meet the moment, and fell far short of what patient, passionate Melburnians deserve.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies

Advertisement

MUSIC

Mozart, Salieri and Pleyel ★★★★

Australian Brandenburg Orchestra, Melbourne Recital Centre, October 17 Billed as “a classical powerhouse”, this program of works by Mozart, Salieri and Ignaz Pleyel sets up an interesting three-way conversation between three accomplished but contrasting contemporaries. Artistic director Paul Dyer conducts from the fortepiano. Laura Manariti Contrary to popular belief, Salieri was an actual admirer of Mozart. However, the Sinfonia from his “heroic-comic” opera Cublai, gran Kan de Tartari (ostensibly based on the life of Kublai Khan) was more reminiscent of Beethoven with its muscular treatment of the predominant triadic material. Mozart’s Divertimento for Stings in D major, K. 136 was given sprightly treatment; broad brushstrokes emphasising its elegantly tapered arcs of melody enhanced by the soft-grained timbre of the period string band.

Advertisement

Only recently attributed to him, Pleyel’s Concerto for Violone in E-flat major is receiving its world premiere performances on this tour by the Australian Brandenburg Orchestra with its own principal bass Robert Nairn as soloist. A precursor of the double bass, the violone has five strings instead of four. This substantial work shows the influence of Pleyel’s teacher Haydn, with its deftly variegated approach to orchestration and rhythm. Nairn rose with aplomb to the concerto’s various technical challenges, not least to playing for the most part in the instrument’s upper register where accurate intonation and well-projected resonance can be harder to achieve. A novel second-movement pizzicato cadenza offset the dramatic “storm and stress” style of the outer movements. A precursor of the double bass, the violone has five strings instead of four. Laura Manariti The dynamo in this powerhouse was undoubtedly Mozart’s Symphony No. 39 in E-flat major, K. 543. Conducted by artistic director Paul Dyer from the fortepiano, this passionately committed account was notable for its elegant poise, balancing moments of rhetorical drama with well-judged wit and bringing to the fore the interplay between the well-coloured strings, wind and brass. Undergirded by buoyant rhythms and razor-sharp passage work, leading to a sudden conclusion, this was the Brandenburg at its brilliant best.

Reviewed by Tony Way

Advertisement

DANCE

Place Dances ★★★★

Buxton Contemporary, Southbank, until October 18 This fascinating new solo work marks a significant return for Lucy Guerin. She largely stopped performing in her own work after launching her company some 25 years ago. Now, as she steps away from that company, she once again steps into the limelight. Place Dances by Lucy Guerin at Buxton Contemporary. Gianna Rizzo It’s a long absence but the interval seems to collapse when she appears: the same quiet, compact, unflappable presence. The same sharp profile and cool expression. The practice of creating and thinking through her body has plainly endured. This is part dance and part lecture, with Guerin tracing the sources of her creativity. Her spoken reflections are presented in an adjoining room, but the sound carries into the main space, as though lecture and dance were neighbouring exhibits.

Advertisement

The dance is like a distillation of her essential impulses as a choreographer: quick, deft gestures, short steps, upright posture and active fingers. The organisation of the space, too, lays bare her tendency to enclose the space, to make stages within the stage. It’s an intriguing companion to NEWRETRO, her expansive 2023 reflection on her work with Lucy Guerin Inc. Both inhabit galleries with austere black-and-white presentations. But this is darker – the act of recollection exposes the doubts that accompany her desires. Guerin’s interest in dialogues between incompatible ideas finds expression in the alternation of lecture and dance. Then, in the middle of the work, there’s a literal dialogue with herself. It’s a conceit that perhaps only her quiet earnestness could make persuasive. For Guerin, imagination is central: the ability to conceive not simply how a body might move, but where. To imagine a body placed in another world, moving through another atmosphere, is the origin of her choreographic endeavours. Crafted with characteristic dramaturgical care, Place Dances offers candid, almost ingenuous reflections on artistic motivations. There are glimpses of gothic melancholy, but it feels like an exciting beginning: a transition with the promise of dances still to come.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann

Advertisement

MUSIC

Macy Gray ★★★

The Encore Tour

Hamer Hall, October 13 Someone in the crowd calls out “Macy!” – another yells “Where are you?” The crowd is getting impatient by this point, starting to clap to entice Macy Gray on to the stage. It’s understandable, given they’ve been waiting for more than an hour, including a 15-minute late start to the event and a dynamic performance from support act Emi Secrest. Macy Gray performs at Melbourne’s Hamer Hall. Martin Philbey Eventually the band walks out, all of them wearing a similar afro wig (perhaps it’s a nod to her signature hair?). Gray finally strolls on stage in a bright orange summer dress and red fingerless gloves, launching into her signature raspy tones to cheers. Gray returns to Australia following a successful 2024 run that celebrated the 25th anniversary of her debut album, On How Life Is. The 2026 The Encore Tour is even more expansive, covering metro and regional venues nationally.

Advertisement

Related Article Take 7 Macy Gray was dumped by her record label while pregnant. Then her career really took off Tuesday’s show was a postponed session from September 11 due to a 24-hour strike by Arts Centre Melbourne staff. Instead of a soulful evening of live music, the public were met with a picket line and public rally. (The industrial dispute has since been resolved after staff accepted an improved pay offer.) The cancelled performance didn’t seem to faze Gray, as she made no mention of it. She continued to swish her skirt, side step and clap her hands to the funky beat. She encouraged the audience to sing and dance along, stating “this ain’t no library”. She reiterates to the audience that she and the band have come all the way from Los Angeles “to hear you sing to us”. Gray with members of her band, who bring a more jazz-inspired approach to her original songs, on stage at Hamer Hall. Martin Philbey The band brings a more jazz-inspired approach to her original tracks, including shifting up the island groove in Witness. She changes the lyrics, encouraging the audience to repeat “and I wish I was Jesus” followed by “I’ll fix it for ya”.

Advertisement

Alongside other originals, such as I’ve Committed Murder, she sings covers of Radiohead’s Creep, Boney M.’s Sunny and Fred Said Right’s I’m Too Sexy. A disgruntled couple leaves early, complaining that they didn’t pay to hear cover songs. The set finishes at 10.50pm – late for a school night. But Gray doesn’t leave without singing her most well-known song, I Try, which gets fans to their feet, and joining in the chorus.

Reviewed by Vyshnavee Wijekumar DANCE

The Sleeping Beauty ★★★★

Regent Theatre, until October 18 The Stuttgart Ballet is in town, offering a rare chance to see a major European company dance one of its signature storybook ballets – with all the old-world charm and seriousness you could want. It’s also a chance to see a handful of genuine international ballet stars. First among them is Elisa Badenes, who danced Aurora on opening night, a dancer with exceptional composure and the silkiest of turns. The Stuttgart Ballet is in town. Kate Longley

Advertisement

Her Prince Désiré was Henrik Erikson: neat as a folded napkin in everything he does. His partnering with Badenes was compelling throughout, culminating in an exquisite grand pas de deux during the marriage festivities. The highlight was a diagonal of supported turns and plunging fish dives where, for one blissful moment, the two dancers appeared so connected, so entirely at one, that it was unclear who was supporting who. The wicked fairy Carabosse was danced by Jason Reilly, a veteran dramatic dynamo. He has a distinctive presence: quick, harassed, mocking, but earnest even when parodying the classical steps of the others. Carabosse has an elevated significance in Marcia Haydée’s version of the ballet. Haydée has transformed the contest between Carabosse and the Lilac Fairy into a sort of epic contest between good and evil. It can seem a little absurd – too much drama for the fey conceit – but this is a production that is very much of its time. Created in 1987, it’s essentially a Cold War fairy tale, showing a world dominated by two great powers. Mizuki Amemiya of The Stuttgart Ballet. Kate Longley

Advertisement

Abigail Willson-Heisel brought unflappable presence to the Lilac Fairy, while among the other dancers, Riccardo Ferlito drew the eye with the height and energy of his leaps as the bare-chested Ali Baba. It’s a long way to travel just to perform The Sleeping Beauty, even if it is a defining production. Once upon a time, they might have brought a second ballet to show another side of their repertoire. But visits by international companies of this stature – any stature, really – are few and far between these days.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann MUSIC

Isata Kanneh-Mason ★★★★

Melbourne Recital Centre, October 9 Navigating a journey from darkness to light, pianist Isata Kanneh-Mason’s Australian debut recital offered plenty of familiar music. Bookended by two of Beethoven’s most popular sonatas, the “Moonlight” and the “Waldstein”, it also included Ravel’s astoundingly imaginative but fiendishly difficult Gaspard de la nuit. Two works by Bulgarian-English composer Dobrinka Tabakova provided a contrasting contemporary aesthetic. Isata Kanneh-Mason performs at Melbourne Recital Centre on October 9, 2026 Laura Manariti

Advertisement

In Beethoven’s famous moonlit opening, Kanneh-Mason’s striking ability for extremely restrained dynamics and tone colour might have suggested a burgeoning sense of drama, yet this remained unrealised. The blazing finale displayed her prodigious technique, even if greater detail could have been revealed with lighter pedalling. Editor's pick Melbourne live reviews Jealousy, friendship and love take centre-stage in this story In Ravel’s brightly hued triptych, the water sprite Ondine splashed around in a luxurious aqueous soundscape while Kanneh-Mason’s trademark restraint lent the scene of the scaffold appropriate eeriness. She also convincingly captured Scarbo’s caprice, mischief and malevolence. After a symbolic change from dark evening gown to shorter pale blue dress, Kanneh-Mason turned to two works by Tabakova, containing the nucleus of the program. Nocturne, an attractive minimalist miniature summoned up night. Using harmonics and repeated notes, Halo effectively evoked a lunar halo which becomes increasingly bright. Clearly close to her heart, Kanneh-Mason played the “Waldstein” with great devotion, ensuring that the finale’s beginning did point to the dawn (an alternative nickname for the work). The blazing sunshine of the closing pages, however, were clouded over by some heavy pedalling.

Advertisement

Impressive as Kanneh-Mason’s playing is, trading some technical brilliance for a wider tonal palette and greater emotional abandon would have taken the performance to a higher level. An over-the-top arrangement of the 1960s hit I Say a Little Prayer for You provided a buoyant encore for the enthusiastic audience.

Reviewed by Tony Way MUSIC

Pekka Kuusisto: Legends and Luminaries ★★★★

Australian Chamber Orchestra, Melbourne Recital Centre, October 10 Ebullience is at the heart of Pekka Kuusisto’s artistic DNA. Joy, passion, commitment and a sense of fun are among the enviable qualities the Finnish violinist and composer brought to his latest collaboration with the Australian Chamber Orchestra. Pekka Kuusisto (left) performs with the Australian Chamber Orchestra. Nic Walker

Advertisement

As guest leader, Kuusisto helmed the orchestra through a program of contrasting styles, all with their own aural appeal. In Kuusisto’s thoughtful arrangement of excerpts from Mozart’s The Magic Flute, a little messiness was the price paid for an overture that ran at bullet train speed. Once the high-octane excitement subsided, beautifully shaped lyrical moments emerged before leading into the Queen of the Night’s aria. Editor's pick Melbourne Fringe Festival Not just red noses and creepy characters: Why it’s time to give clowning another chance Written for Kuusisto and premiered with the ACO Collective in 2019, American composer Nico Muhly’s Shrink: Concerto for Violin and Strings is a tour de force that is a perfect fit for the dedicatee’s mercurial personality. Across the work’s 22 minutes, Muhly weaves an intricate, compelling tapestry of textures, while the soloist jumps through every technical hoop imaginable. Kuusisto clearly thrives on such challenges, bringing unflagging zeal and a wealth of colour and emotion to the cleverly constructed score that exploits narrowing intervals alluded to in the title. Receiving its first Australian performances on this tour, Pulitzer Prize-winning composer Ellen Reid’s “paean to the Californian landscape”, West Coast Sky Eternal elicited an empathetic performance. Its shifting textural perspectives are intriguing at first before an extended pizzicato passage tends to unbalance its structure.

Advertisement

Clearly revelling in Kuusisto’s leadership, an arrangement of Mendelssohn’s String Quintet No. 2 in B-flat, Op. 87 received classic ACO treatment. Ebullience certainly radiated through the outer movements, while an elegant second-movement scherzando preceded an exquisite, heart-tugging slow movement. A superbly judged encore came with Reger’s arrangement of one of Bach’s most intimately rhapsodic works for organ, the chorale prelude O Mensch, bewein’.

Reviewed by Tony Way The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

text:

Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Rare earths strike in NT extends 8km beyond previous Barkly hits Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward October 19, 2026 — 1:13pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Barkly Rare Earths has continued its impressive exploration success, hitting significant rare earths mineralisation in 13 of 16 additional holes at its flagship Barkly rare earths project in the Northern Territory. The latest results from its 10,000-metre phase-one drilling campaign have pushed the boundaries of known mineralisation another eight kilometres into previously untested ground. Significant rare earths intercepts have now been recorded in 56 of the 60 holes assayed, spread across a whopping 23km and delivering an impressive strike rate of more than 93 per cent. A reverse circulation drill rig in action at Barkly Rare Earths’ phase-one drilling campaign targeting a massive expansion of its existing 40-million-tonne rare earth resource in the Northern Territory. The drilling program is designed to test for extensions to the project’s existing 40 million-tonne inferred mineral resource grading 2100 parts per million (ppm) total rare earth oxides (TREO). The current inventory is split between the northern and southern deposits, leaving almost 15km of virtually untouched ground in between for the drill bit to explore. That sizeable gap helps explain Barkly’s lofty exploration target of between 200 million and one billion tonnes at a grade of between 1600ppm and 1900ppm TREO. The results served up another swag of eye-catching TREO grades, reinforcing the project’s potential amid accelerating global investment in non-Chinese critical minerals supply chains.

Advertisement

‘This is an intercept rate over 90 per cent across the 60 phase-one holes reported so far, in holes up to 23 kilometres apart.’ Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright The four highest-grade new assays from the latest batch all came from the project’s southern reaches, within and around its existing mineral resource. The standout hole struck a 1.5-metre intercept grading 2171ppm TREO from a shallow 10.5m, including a cracking 0.5-metre section assaying 4550ppm TREO and 1678 magnet rare earth oxides (MREO) from 10.5m. Another notable hit included 2.5m running 1774ppm TREO from 20.5m, which contained a richer slice of 0.5m going a 2599ppm TREO and 845ppm MREO from 21m. Further northwest, five of the first eight holes drilled 8km from previous intercepts also returned significant mineralisation, including the widest phase-one intercept to date of 5.5m at 1035ppm TREO and 343ppm MREO from just 22m downhole. Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright said: “We have now intersected rare earth mineralisation in the northwest, outside the exploration target and six to eight kilometres from previously reported mineralised intercepts. In the south, all eight holes returned significant intercepts... It gives me real confidence in the scale of what we are drilling at Barkly, and we are tendering for a second rig so we can build out the resource faster.”

Advertisement

The company says drilling continues to confirm the deposit’s key characteristics; it appears laterally extensive, with the mineralised horizon now intersected across a massive 23 km. It is shallow and flat-lying, with hits between surface and 38m downhole and is rich in high-value magnet rare earth oxides (MREO), which make up a healthy 29 to 38 per cent of the TREO in the new intercepts. Management says this is consistent with the 34 per cent MREO ratio of the existing inferred mineral resource. MREO’s include neodymium, praseodymium, terbium and dysprosium, some of the most sought-after of the 17 rare earth elements. They are essential for manufacturing high-strength permanent magnets used in electric vehicles and wind turbines. Notably, uranium and thorium levels remain consistently low, between one and three ppm and five to 11 ppm, respectively. Low levels of these radioactive elements are a significant advantage, potentially simplifying processing and reducing costs. The results come as Australia and its allies crank up the race to secure critical minerals supplies and loosen China’s grip on the global rare earths market. The Federal Government recently trumpeted the start of construction at Arafura Rare Earths’ Nolans project, also in the Northern Territory, which has attracted A$1.2 billion in government backing and is tipped to eventually meet up to five per cent of global rare earths demand.

Advertisement

With Australia and the United States committing billions to building alternative supply chains, the geopolitical stars appear to be aligning for explorers such as Barkly. To date, the company has drilled 89 holes for 2168 metres, including 6 re-drills. Samples from a further 26 holes are at or being prepared for the lab, including two re-drills of assayed holes. The company is also progressing with concentration and extraction testwork, with a mineral resource update targeted for the fourth quarter of this year. Barkly is also tendering for a second drill rig to speed up the campaign. With a hit rate that would make a West Perth miner blush and a mineralised footprint that now stretches over 23km, Barkly is systematically building a case for a project of serious scale. As Australia and its allies plough billions into securing non-Chinese rare earths supply, the company’s timing looks impeccable. And as a second drill rig rolls in, the market may not have long to wait to see how big this story could get. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Low-cost carrier Vietjet’s hopes of expanding into Australia’s domestic market have hit a snag, after the United Kingdom High Court granted an order to freeze the carrier’s assets as part of a fight with a hedge fund seeking to recover debts. FW Aviation, an aircraft leasing company registered in Jersey, secured court orders against the airline for $US250 million ($360 million) for four Airbus A321s in London late last week. Vietjet’s inaugural Ho Chi Minh City to Sydney flight in 2023. The order follows a long-running battle by a private investment fund FitzWalter Capital, which controls FW Aviation, to get the Vietnam-based Vietjet to pay for the use of the four planes. UK courts have ordered three judgments against Vietjet, for $18.8 million (in 2024), $182 million (in 2025) and $18.3 million (in a third trial), with the airline making a partial $2 million payment in 2025.

Advertisement

In the latest case, the business and property division of Britain’s High Court heard how Vietjet has resisted paying, and even halted flights of aircraft to Singapore where they would have been seized under court orders. “In October 2021, following Vietjet’s continuing failure to pay rent for its use of the aircraft (during the COVID lockdowns), the lenders served notices on Vietjet seeking to terminate the sub-lease agreements,” the court ruling reads. “Shortly thereafter, FWA acquired all rights formerly held by the lenders,” which included the right to recover sums owed under sub-lease agreements and custody and control of the aircraft, the court said. Vietjet raised eyebrows with its stunt featuring flight attendants dressed in bikinis. Justice Pushpinder Saini found that Vietjet’s actions constituted a “risk of dissipation”, or danger that a defendant will hide, transfer, or sell assets before a court judgment can be enforced.

Advertisement

This masthead understands the prospect of legal judgments against Vietjet would likely complicate its bid to receive permission to operate as a domestic airline. Vietjet has been approached for comment. Related Article Aviation A first look at Western Sydney airport’s new international lounge The low-cost carrier has applied to the Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA) for an air operator’s certificate, which would allow it to operate on domestic routes in Australia. It’s expected to operate up to 10 Boeing 737s on routes between Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane, under the name Cherrie Air. CASA said the Civil Aviation Act allows it “to conduct financial viability assessments as part of the [AOC] application process”. “CASA does conduct these assessments, particularly for AOC applications for large air transport operations,” it said.

Advertisement

Vietjet, which was Vietnam’s first privately owned airline when it began flying in 2011, has made network expansion a priority, operating divisions in Thailand and as far away as Kazakhstan. The company has previously raised eyebrows for stunts featuring women dressed only in bikinis. Vietjet is also expected to become the third international airline offering flights from Western Sydney International – after Air New Zealand and Singapore Airlines. It’s slated to begin flying between Western Sydney and Ho Chi Minh City on 10 January 2027, operating two return services per week, on Wednesdays and Sundays. Its website shows prices for those flights from WSI to Ho Chi Minh ranging from $34 to $411. Vietjet’s international arm – based out of Vietnam – currently operates daily return flights to Ho Chi Minh City from Sydney and Melbourne. Brisbane and Perth are connected to Ho Chi Minh City with five and three weekly return flights, respectively. title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
